canonical.summary: Initial sudden yellowing/browning and wilting of plants followed by death; a brown to black lesion or canker develops at the base of the stem near the soil line and can girdle the stem, causing sudden permanent wilt. Under high humidity a dense white mat of mycelium develops on the stem base and surrounding soil, and low-hanging fruit touching infested soil develop a wet rot and rapid decay.
diagnostic_features: A white mat of mycelium at the base of the stem at the soil line, with numerous small (1 to 2 mm), round, tan-to-reddish brown (later dark brown) spherical sclerotia developing on the surface of the mycelium.
treatments: Avoid planting in fields with a history of southern blight.
Rotate host crops with non-host crops such as corn, wheat, or barley; rotation with graminaceous crops can reduce S. rolfsii inoculum in the soil.
Modify planting dates to avoid conditions that favor disease development.
Remove and destroy symptomatic plants (and reduce or eliminate weed populations).
Deep plow (>4 inches) to bury infected plant debris and sclerotia and invert the soil.
Ensure the previous crop is fully decomposed prior to planting.
Maintain adequate soil pH for plant growth (lower soil pH encourages disease).
Avoid moving infested soil to clean fields.
Use certified, pathogen-free seed to avoid introducing inoculum to non-infested soil.
Soil solarization (reduces sclerotia viability at 50-55C / 122-131F for up to 6 hours) and anaerobic soil disinfestation.
Biological control agents such as Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma viride, and certain mycorrhizal fungi.
Soil fumigants including chloropicrin, metam-sodium (sodium metam sodium), and allyl isothiocyanate.
Grafting onto resistant rootstocks (e.g., tomato rootstocks 'Maxifort', 'Big Power', 'Beaufort'); host resistance is otherwise not currently a viable option.

Labeled fungicides: pre-plant pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB) and flutolanil; strobilurins (pyraclostrobin, azoxystrobin, fluoxastrobin); SDHIs (fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin, penthiopyrad); triazoles (tebuconazole, prothioconazole). Efficacy can be variable.

canonical.summary: Coarse white fan-shaped mycelium grows on lower stems, pods, and soil, with tan to brown round sclerotia later forming; early symptoms include wilting or yellowing of individual branches or the main stem, and brown canker-like stem lesions near the crown that kill colonized, dark brown, brittle, shredded stems and crowns.
diagnostic_features: Coarse white mycelium in a distinctive fan-shaped pattern and tan to brown spherical sclerotia 0.5 to 1.5 mm in diameter; stem lesions the color of a brown paper bag with a canker-like appearance, and colonized stems/crowns that are dark brown, brittle, and shredded.
treatments: Rotations of two years or more to a non-host crop to prevent inoculum build-up (longer rotations needed once high inoculum is established); avoid rotations with soybean, tobacco, melons, and vegetables
Maintain weed control during rotations to prevent increase on susceptible species
Plant cultivars with good partial resistance and avoid highly susceptible cultivars
Avoid excess canopy development and over-irrigation; avoid in-season cultivation that uncovers buried sclerotia and throws infested soil onto plants
Use deep plowing to bury debris and sclerotia of S. rolfsii

Apply fungicides with good activity against stem rot, first at 45 to 75 days after planting (45 to 60 days most common), with at least one additional application 14 to 28 days later (up to four applications at 2 to 4 week intervals where severe)
Spray plants at night when leaves are folded to expose stems and crowns
Apply fungicides in-furrow or in banded sprays within 3 to 4 weeks after emergence to enhance control

canonical.summary: Lesions develop under the calyx as small, light brown spots at the stem end that enlarge quickly and invade the rest of the fruit, becoming covered with dark mycelium bearing many gray spores; the fruit eventually becomes totally covered and mummified. Blossoms may show blasting (browning and drying) extending down the pedicel.
diagnostic_features: Infected fruit becomes covered with gray spores and mycelium, giving a velvety gray appearance; large numbers of spores are released as visible gray puffs when disturbed; mummified berries become dry, tough, and covered with a gray, dusty powder.
treatments: Manage by combined cultural and chemical methods (no highly resistant commercial cultivars exist)
Choose cultivars with upright growth or a reflexed calyx to lower infection risk
Select a planting site with good soil drainage, air circulation, and direct sunlight; orient rows with prevailing wind to speed drying
Space plants adequately and use raised beds to improve airflow and drainage
Use plastic or straw mulch to reduce rain splash, fruit-soil contact, weeds, and canopy moisture
Avoid over-fertilizing; excess nitrogen (especially in spring before harvest) increases fruit rot and dense foliage
Use drip irrigation to eliminate excess moisture on fruit and leaves; maintain good weed control
Remove senescent/dead tissue in early spring just before bloom, and remove diseased fruit from under the canopy to reduce inoculum
Pick fruit frequently and early in the day once plants are dry; handle berries carefully to avoid bruising; cull diseased berries and remove them from the field
Cool/refrigerate fruit promptly (≈32–50°F / keep ~34°F) and raise CO₂ (12–15%) during shipping to suppress B. cinerea
Apply fungicides during the critical early and full bloom period; rotate chemistries, use tank mixes, and follow label restrictions to manage resistance
Alternate single-site botryticides (Elevate, Kenja, Luna, Switch) with multi-site protectants (Captan, Thiram); use the Strawberry Advisory System (StAS) to time sprays

summary.quote: Lesions typically develop under the calyx as small, light brown spots (Figures 1 and 2) that enlarge quickly and invade the rest of the fruit (Figure 3). Lesions become fully covered with dark mycelium bearing many gray spores (conidia) (Figure 4).

canonical.summary: Swollen or puffy portions appear on newly expanding leaves, shoots, buds or flowers, turning into galls that range in color from green, silvery white, to pink or red, which later develop a white surface growth and eventually turn brown and shrivel.
diagnostic_features: A white coating of microscopic, spore-forming structures develops on swollen, galled plant tissue; galling is generally most abundant on the lower portions of the plant, and late in the season infected tissue turns brown, dry, and hard.
treatments: Hand pick or clip off and dispose of galled tissue before it develops a covering of white, spore-forming structures.
Prune hosts or hand pick galls only when conditions and foliage are dry.
Avoid overhead watering; irrigate using drip emitters or by flooding soil.
Avoid crowding plants and provide good air circulation around them.
Reduce greenhouse humidity.
Avoid planting highly susceptible cultivars and select less susceptible cultivars.
Apply the first spray before budbreak in spring and the second spray 2 to 3 weeks later.
Apply a preventive copper fungicide such as Bordeaux mixture (e.g., Bordeaux 6-2-100), Badge X2, Bonide Copper Fungicide, Monterey Liqui-Cop, or Nu-Cop 50 DF, before foggy conditions or rainfall.
Apply Captan 80 WDG at 1.5 lb/100 gal water.
Apply mancozeb-based products (e.g., Fore 80WP Rainshield, Protect DF) with a spreader-sticker.

These areas turn into galls that range in color from green, silvery white, to pink or red depending on the part of the plant infected. As these galls age, they develop a white surface growth which consists of a layer of reproductive spores. Eventually, the infected plant part will turn brown and shrivel up into hard galls.

canonical.summary: Leaf spots first appear as small dark or chlorotic flecks that darken and enlarge into circular, 1 to 10 mm dark brown to black lesions, sometimes with a chlorotic halo; sporulation (tufts of conidia, sometimes in concentric circles) occurs mostly on the lower (abaxial) leaf surface, and infected leaflets turn yellow and defoliate.
diagnostic_features: Lesions are dark brown to nearly black and may lack the prominent yellow halo of early leaf spot; on the UNDERSIDE of the leaf a dark/velvety mass of spores gives the spot a velvety, raised or tufted appearance visible without magnification, and diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of spores on the lower surface of the lesion.
treatments: Crop rotation of 2 to 4 years with non-peanut crops to delay disease onset and let debris decompose; rotate away from old/infected crops and avoid planting downwind
Control peanut volunteers in rotation crops and remove volunteer plants from the last crop
Plant runner and Virginia-type cultivars with moderate partial resistance to leaf spots
Collect and burn or bury crop debris; conservation (strip) tillage can reduce leaf spot pressure; early planting (late April to early May) can slow spread
Apply fungicides preventively, beginning at very early pod stage (R3) or ~30 DAP (no later than 45 DAP); typically 4 to 7 applications per season
Reapply every 14 days or per the leaf spot advisory (disease advisories based on rainfall/temperature/RH); continue until 14 to 21 days before harvest

Use chlorothalonil or copper fungicides; apply fungicides of different modes of action in alternation, tank mixes, or pre-mixes, using a non-selective (group M) fungicide as the final spray of the season

canonical.summary: Early leaf spot typically causes penetrating brown lesions (spots) visible on the upper and lower leaf surface, usually surrounded by a yellow halo, and produces tufts of silvery, hair-like spores on the upper lesion surface during humid weather. Lesions are about the diameter of a no. 2 pencil and almost orange on the lower leaf surface.
diagnostic_features: Early leaf spot lesions are brown (versus dark-brown-to-black for late leaf spot), most apparent on the underside of the leaf, with a prominent yellow halo; the fungus produces tufts of silvery, hair-like spores on the UPPER lesion surface, and diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of spores on the upper surface of the lesion.
treatments: Crop rotation of 3 years or more with any crop other than peanut to reduce disease severity; rotate as far as possible from old/infected crops and avoid planting downwind
Control peanut volunteers in rotation crops and remove volunteer plants from the last crop
Plant cultivars with partial/moderate resistance (e.g., Virginia-type cultivars such as Bailey and Sullivan)
Collect and burn or bury crop debris so it decomposes before replanting; conservation (strip) tillage can reduce leaf spot pressure
In leaf-spot-prone fields, early planting (late April to early May) can slow disease spread
Apply fungicides preventively, beginning at very early pod stage (R3) or ~30-35 days after planting (no later than 45 DAP)
Reapply fungicides every 14 days or according to the leaf spot advisory
Use chlorothalonil or copper fungicides; mix or alternate fungicides from different FRAC/resistance groups and use non-selective (group M) fungicides for two or more sprays per season

profiles.disease: Phomopsis Leaf Blight And Fruit Rot

canonical.summary: Phomopsis leaf blight first appears as circular, reddish to purple spots (about 3/8 to 1/2 inch in diameter) on mature leaves; lesion centers turn gray or tan as they mature, and spots enlarge to become V-shaped, delineated by major leaf veins, potentially causing severe defoliation.
diagnostic_features: Older lesions develop a characteristic pattern of three color zones — a pale brown or tan center surrounded by a brown ring, surrounded by a ring of dark brown, red, or purple; numerous black pycnidia develop in the center of the spot, and merged lesions form angular or V-shaped discolorations limited by major veins.
treatments: Obtain certified disease-free strawberry plants from a reputable, commercial supplier.
Plant strawberries in a sunny, open location and on a shallow berm or mound of raised soil.
Avoid crowding plants and control nearby weeds to increase air circulation and reduce leaf spot diseases.
Use drip or furrow irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if irrigating overhead, apply water in the morning so foliage dries rapidly.
Carefully manage irrigation to avoid prolonged soggy soil (waterlogging).
At the end of the growing season, remove and dispose of strawberry debris away from where strawberries will be grown the next season.
Consider growing strawberries as an annual instead of a perennial.
Apply potassium silicate and calcium silicate separately as a soil treatment combined with foliar spray.
Broad spectrum fungicides (captan, thiram) offer some control, and fungicides with a specific mode of action (e.g., Rally, possibly the QoI/strobilurins) also offer control.

In matted row systems, apply broad spectrum fungicides or mixes after harvest until late summer, followed by mowing of older leaves to reduce inoculum (only effective if leaves are later removed or tilled into the soil).
Fungicides are generally not effective or warranted for Phomopsis leaf blight of strawberry in home gardens.

diagnostic_features.quote: Older lesions develop a characteristic pattern of three colors zones, commonly a pale brown or tan center surrounded by a brown ring that is surrounded by a ring of dark brown, red, or purple.

treatments.value: Obtain certified disease-free strawberry plants from a reputable, commercial supplier.; Plant strawberries in a sunny, open location and on a shallow berm or mound of raised soil.; Avoid crowding plants and control nearby weeds to increase air circulation and reduce leaf spot diseases.; Use drip or furrow irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; if irrigating overhead, apply water in the morning so foliage dries rapidly.; Carefully manage irrigation to avoid prolonged soggy soil (waterlogging).; At the end of the growing season, remove and dispose of strawberry debris away from where strawberries will be grown the next season.; Consider growing strawberries as an annual instead of a perennial.; Apply potassium silicate and calcium silicate separately as a soil treatment combined with foliar spray.; Broad spectrum fungicides (captan, thiram) offer some control, and fungicides with a specific mode of action (e.g., Rally, possibly the QoI/strobilurins) also offer control.; In matted row systems, apply broad spectrum fungicides or mixes after harvest until late summer, followed by mowing of older leaves to reduce inoculum (only effective if leaves are later removed or tilled into the soil).; Fungicides are generally not effective or warranted for Phomopsis leaf blight of strawberry in home gardens.
treatments.quote: Broad spectrum fungicides (captan, thiram) offer some control and fungicides with a specific mode of action also offer control (e.g. Rally, possibly the QoI or strobilurins). In matted row systems, the application of broad spectrum fungicides or mixes after harvest until late summer may be effective, followed by mowing of older leaves to reduce inoculum; this strategy is ineffective unless leaves are later removed or tilled into the soil.

canonical.summary: The most common symptoms on peppers are crown rot and fruit rot, with wilting of plants under wet conditions followed by plant death; crown lesions become dark brown and girdle the stem, and fruit rot appears as water-soaked areas covered with white powdery to cottony mold.
diagnostic_features: Crown lesions become dark brown and extend upward to girdle the stem; fruit rot appears as water-soaked areas eventually covered with white powdery to cottony mold.
treatments: Plant resistant varieties. There are some bell, sweet, and hot peppers with moderate resistance to P. capsici.
Plant in field with good drainage and even terrain that will not promote having standing water for prolonged periods of time.
Use raised beds and plastic mulch whenever possible.
Do not use surface water (ponds, creek) for irrigation since it may be infested.
Irrigate moderately from a well via drip, and avoid overhead irrigation especially once fruit is present.
Monitor fields for disease. Remove diseased fruit or plants away from the field.
Do not leave culls in the field or near surface irrigation water sources (ponds, creeks).
Harvest fruit as soon as possible from problem fields.
Sanitize farm equipment after working on an infested field.
Rotate to crops that are not hosts of P. capsici (cereals).
Soil applications of fungicide at transplant followed by drip applications offer higher protection against Phytophthora root and crown rot.
Sprays ensuring good coverage may be needed to protect fruit in heavily infested sites.
Alternate products to avoid generating fungicide-resistant strains.

Example fungicide products: Cyazofamid (Ranman 400 SC), Ametoctradin + dimethomorph (Zampro), Fluopicolide (Presidio), Mandipropamid (Revus), Mefenoxam + copper (Ridomil Gold/Copper), Famoxadone + cymoxanil (Tanos 50WG), Fluazinam (Omega 500 F).
The only OMRI labeled active ingredients that have some efficacy against P. capsici are fixed copper formulations.
Home gardeners have no effective chemical control options and must rely completely on host resistance and cultural strategies.

canonical.summary: Lesions are small (less than 1/4 inch) and white; diamond to lens-shaped on vines, petioles and leaf veins, and round on fruit and leaves. Lesions coalesce until vines and leaf petioles turn white and foliage dies, and fruit develops white, tan, or silver russeting.
diagnostic_features: Lesions are white with a very distinctive diamond to spindle (lens) shape that is characteristic for the disease; leaf tissue between veins is not affected, and dead vines become so brittle they shatter when stepped on.
look_alikes: normal fruit rot problems associated with wet weather
treatments: Rotate with nonhost crops for at least 3 years to reduce soil inoculum (the pathogen can survive in soil).
Choose sunny, well-drained sites with good air circulation to encourage rapid drying of the foliage.
Space plants and orient rows with the prevailing wind to aid ventilation and drying of leaf surfaces.
Use drip/trickle irrigation, or time overhead irrigation to minimize leaf wetness.
Scout fields for disease, especially after rainy weather, and apply protectant fungicides when disease first occurs / beginning at fruit set.

Apply fungicides such as chlorothalonil (Bravo), Dithane (mancozeb), and strobilurins like trifloxystrobin (Flint), Cabrio, Quadris/Satori, Merivon, and Amistar; thorough coverage of foliage, vines, and fruit is necessary, with a 7-day interval during rainy weather.
Promptly remove and destroy diseased plant material during the season and plow under / deep plow crop residue after harvest to bury inoculum.
Manage weeds and potential alternative hosts.
Avoid movement of infested soil to clean fields and inspect any pumpkin fruit brought onto the farm to re-stock pick-your-own fields.

On fruit, P. tabacinum causes white, tan, or silver russeting which can merge to form a continuous dry, scabby surface.

canonical.summary: Circular patches of affected turf ranging from 3 to 26 ft in diameter, with leaves at the patch periphery appearing bright yellow and/or orange; leaf sheaths show water-soaked, reddish-brown, or black lesions and foliar dieback spreads from leaf tip toward the base.
diagnostic_features: Circular patches 3 to 26 ft in diameter with bright yellow and/or orange leaves at the periphery; a soft, dark rot at the base of the leaf with a rotted odor and leaves that easily pull off the stem; leaf sheath lesions (water-soaked, reddish-brown, or black); patch centers become thin and sunken and may be invaded by weeds.
look_alikes: brown patch (R. solani AG 1-A on cool season grasses)
treatments: Establish a turfgrass species best adapted to your geographical area and situation

Avoid excessive nitrogen during disease development periods; use slow-release nitrogen rather than readily available forms; apply a balanced fertilizer with equivalent potassium and nitrogen based on an updated soil test; do not apply nitrogen before 4-in. soil temperatures are consistently 65 °F and rising
Regulate moisture in the thatch and soil: install drainage tile, modify soil profile for porosity, and cultivate/core aerate to reduce compaction and thatch
Control traffic patterns to prevent compaction; where air movement and sunlight are low, prune or remove surrounding trees and shrubs
Irrigate deeply no more than once a week and only as necessary, during early morning hours (2:00–8:00 a.m.) when dew is already present
Keep mowing height consistent and correct for the turf variety; mow diseased areas last and wash all turf clippings off the mower before the next site

Apply fungicides (commercial turf classes): carboxamides, benzimidazoles, carbamates, dicarboximides, DMI fungicides, di-nitro anilines, nitriles, polyoxins, and Qo inhibitors; specific options include azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, fludioxonil, flutolanil, iprodione, mancozeb, metconazole, myclobutanil, polyoxin D, propiconazole, pyraclostrobin, thiophanate-methyl, thiram, triadimefon, trifloxystrobin, triticonazole, and vinclozolin; apply preventatively in fall when thatch temperature drops below 69.8 °F

canonical.summary: On tomatoes the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions; peppers form small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots on foliage. Heavily infected leaves brown, roll, and wilt, seedlings form a "shepherd's crook" and die, and fruit shows yellow ringspots and brown necrotic sunken areas.
diagnostic_features: Lesions caused by TSWV have blurred margins, while the margins of lesions caused by other diseases are definite.
treatments: Deploy TSWV resistant varieties — select varieties with the Sw-5 (tomato) and Tsw (pepper) genes.
Treat transplants with imidacloprid just before setting in the field to suppress primary spread.
Use reflective mulch.
Control weeds such as dandelions, sow thistle, chickweed, buttercup, and plantain.
Segregate externally sourced plant material; quarantine newly purchased plants; inspect transplants and discard symptomatic plants.
Use biological control: minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and big-eyed bugs (Geocoris punctipes).
Minimize thrips entry in greenhouses with thrips-proof screening on air intakes and vents.
Monitor thrips in the greenhouse with sticky yellow card traps.
Avoid growing ornamentals and vegetables in the same greenhouse.
Home gardeners: spray early in the season with neem oil or other botanical insecticides; summer oil or insecticidal soap may be used.

summary.quote: On tomatoes infected with TSWV, the uppermost leaves appear bronzed with small brown lesions (Figure 1). Infected peppers form small brown necrotic spots and/or chlorotic ring spots on the foliage (Figure 2). Infected foliage on both tomatoes and peppers may become covered with so many spots that the entire leaf browns, rolls, and wilts. Infected seedlings form a “shepherd’s crook” appearance and die (Figure 3).

canonical.summary: Black, fuzzy, round or elongated lesions are produced on susceptible tissues (leaves, green twigs, and shucks) that become infected, which can result in defoliation, reduced stem growth, and nut loss.
diagnostic_features: Black, fuzzy, round or elongated lesions on leaves, green twigs, and shucks.
treatments: The most effective methods for pecan scab management are the use of resistant cultivars and the use of fungicides.
Purchase cultivars that not only have resistance to scab but that are also suited for Mississippi's climate
Plant trees in a location that has good sunlight and airflow.
Homeowners with already established pecan trees may be able to reduce the level of scab that occurs annually by increasing the airflow and sunlight available to the trees.
Fungicides should be applied before the occurrence of conditions that are favorable for disease development.
Fungicide applications are often needed every 2 to 3 weeks, depending on rainfall frequency, over a 5- to 6-month period during the growing season each year
Use multiple fungicides over the course of the season by alternating (rotating) the fungicide being applied at each application.
Fungicides must be rotated according to their designated fungicide group (FRAC group, listed on the product label)

canonical.summary: Minute water-soaked spots appear on the lower surface of leaves and calyxes, enlarging into translucent angular spots delineated by small veins; under high humidity they exude a viscous bacterial ooze drying to a whitish scaly film, with lesions coalescing into reddish-brown to necrotic spots on the upper leaf surface surrounded by a chlorotic halo.
diagnostic_features: The angular lesion shape is defined by leaf veins and veinlets (rather than round like fungal spots), and the lesions are translucent when held up to bright/transmitted light but dark green and water-soaked when viewed with reflected light.
look_alikes: injury caused by some pesticides or other chemical sprays
treatments: Use pathogen-free / certified planting material (best control measure)
Minimize overhead sprinkler/irrigation use, especially during plant establishment and freeze protection; use drip irrigation instead
Use protective structures such as high plastic tunnels or floating row covers as an alternative to overhead water for freeze protection
Avoid moving equipment or harvesters through wet foliage; handle/harvest infested fields after non-infested fields to limit spread
Choose a planting site with good air circulation and sun exposure, control weeds, and use straw mulch to reduce water splash and promote foliage drying
Rotate crops to avoid infesting fields
Soil-incorporate strawberry debris under serious disease conditions to optimize tissue breakdown

Apply registered copper-based products (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, basic copper sulfate, cuprous oxide) at low rates; copper hydroxide formulations may be more effective than copper sulfate, applied early/preventively before warm temperatures to avoid phytotoxicity
Preventive weekly copper applications at 0.3 lb of metallic copper per acre reduced symptoms without phytotoxicity
Apply Actigard (plant-resistance activator) to induce plant defenses and suppress bacterial colonization

summary.value: Minute water-soaked spots appear on the lower surface of leaves and calyxes, enlarging into translucent angular spots delineated by small veins; under high humidity they exude a viscous bacterial ooze drying to a whitish scaly film, with lesions coalescing into reddish-brown to necrotic spots on the upper leaf surface surrounded by a chlorotic halo.
summary.quote: Infection first appears as minute, water-soaked spots on the lower surface of leaves and calyxes. The lesions enlarge to form translucent, angular spots that are delineated by small veins and under conditions of high humidity will exude a viscous ooze of bacteria and bacterial exudates, which appears as a whitish and scaly film after drying. As the disease progresses, lesions coalesce and reddish-brown spots, which later become necrotic, appear on the upper surface of the leaves. A chlorotic halo usually surrounds the infected area.

diagnostic_features.value: The angular lesion shape is defined by leaf veins and veinlets (rather than round like fungal spots), and the lesions are translucent when held up to bright/transmitted light but dark green and water-soaked when viewed with reflected light.
diagnostic_features.quote: One identifying characteristic is the translucent nature of lesions when leaves are held up to a bright light; looking from the backside, light will pass through the angular lesions. ... Another important distinguishing characteristic of Angular leaf spot is that the lesions are translucent when viewed with transmitted light but dark green and water-soaked when viewed with reflected light.

look_alikes.value: common leaf spot; leaf scorch; crown rot; Botrytis gray mold; abiotic injury; fungal leaf spots; injury caused by some pesticides or other chemical sprays
look_alikes.quote: is often confused with common leaf spot and leaf scorch diseases. ... To avoid confusing symptoms of abiotic injury or fungal infection to those of bacterial leaf spot, the shape of the lesion is important to note. The lesion shape of angular leaf spot is defined by leaf veins and veinlets, so during fairly early stages the shape is angular rather than the round shape typical of fungal leaf spots or injury caused by some pesticides or other chemical sprays.

canonical.summary: Symptoms appear only on fruit, beginning as a slight water-soaked, light-tan area on or near the blossom end (occasionally the side); the affected area darkens and enlarges in a widening circle, becoming dark brown or black, shrunken, and dry with a leathery appearance, and affected fruit ripen faster than normal.
diagnostic_features: The lesion forms specifically at the blossom end or bottom side of the fruit and is dry and leathery (tan-colored on pepper), becoming soft only if secondary bacteria and fungi invade; unlike sunscald, it can occur on fruit surfaces not exposed to the sun.
treatments: Test soil to determine whether calcium levels fall within the recommended range
Apply lime to fields known to be low in calcium, preferably in fall, to adjust soil pH to 6.5-7 (mix thoroughly into the top 8-to-12 inches of soil)
Use gypsum (land plaster) at 500 to 1000 pounds per acre as a supplement to liming on calcium-deficient soils, applied several months in advance of planting
Spray foliage and stems with anhydrous calcium chloride (or foliar calcium nitrate / calcium chloride dihydrate with a surfactant) on a weekly schedule during fruiting when symptoms first appear
Regulate and maintain even soil moisture, wetting all soil in the root zone at least every 7 to 10 days
Mulch with black plastic or loose organic material to maintain even soil moisture
Provide proper drainage; do not plant where drainage is poor, surface water accumulates, or soil is droughty
If cultivation is necessary, keep it shallow to avoid root pruning
Fertilize only moderately and avoid products high in potassium, sodium, magnesium, and ammonium, which compete with calcium for uptake
Ensure good air movement through plant spacing and pruning
Choose tolerant cultivars (for peppers, shorter, rounder varieties tend to have more tolerance)
Remove affected fruits when symptoms are first observed to aid development of other fruit on the plant

summary.value: Symptoms appear only on fruit, beginning as a slight water-soaked, light-tan area on or near the blossom end (occasionally the side); the affected area darkens and enlarges in a widening circle, becoming dark brown or black, shrunken, and dry with a leathery appearance, and affected fruit ripen faster than normal.

diagnostic_features: Pink, salmon, or orange-colored masses of spores may form in the lesion under humid conditions; the combination of signs (spores) and symptoms is diagnostic for this disease. During wet weather, lesions on fruit become covered with sticky, light orange ooze composed of millions of conidia.
treatments: Use disease-free plants — the most important management strategy; obtain transplants from pathogen-free/certified nurseries (exclusion)
Use micropropagated plants entered into a strict plant certification program
Plant resistant/tolerant cultivars (e.g. Sweet Charlie less susceptible to fruit rot; NCSU 'BISH'; Florida 'Sensation/Florida 127', 'Florida Brilliance', 'Florida Ember')
Monitor/scout fields, especially during warm and wet weather, for early detection
Remove and destroy (bury or burn) infected plants and surrounding plants within a 5–10 foot radius
Keep nitrogen at required levels (avoid excess); use calcium nitrate instead of ammonium sources
Keep foliage dry, reduce water splash with drip irrigation, and avoid excess overhead irrigation
Avoid moving personnel/equipment from infested to clean areas without proper cleaning; pick infested areas last; do not work plants when wet
Rotate out of strawberries for 2 to 3 years; kill all plants at end of harvest if anthracnose fruit rot was present
Apply preventive/protectant fungicides (e.g. captan) at higher label rates during the critical bloom and Jan–Mar period; add curative products (e.g. Switch, Miravis Prime) when needed

canonical.summary: Plants turn yellow, wilt, and become stunted; the crown shows light water-soaked areas that darken into a dark brown necrotic rot of the crown and upper tap root, and infected plants break off easily at or just below the soil line. Fruit in contact with soil can rot pre- and post-harvest.
diagnostic_features: A characteristic dark brown necrotic rot of the crown and upper tap root; infected plants break off easily at or just below the soil line; the root cortex sloughs off but fibrous vascular tissue remains; white or pink mycelial growth on the lower stem at the soil line in hot, humid weather; on fruit, a dry (not mushy) rot that can form a bulls-eye pattern.
treatments: Rotate out of squash and other cucurbits for 4 years (the fungus survives 2-3 years in soil as chlamydospores)
Avoid fields with a history of severe Fusarium disease and select fields with good water drainage
Avoid over-irrigation; deficit irrigation (reducing water by no more than 40%) early in the season reduces disease, but do not limit water when fruit is setting
Use laboratory-tested, pathogen-free seed and plant fungicide-treated seed (e.g. Maxim 4FS, Group 12)
Avoid injury of fruit during harvest, packing, and transport
Apply biological/biofungicide soil treatments such as Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Rootshield WP, Stargus, or Bexfond as drenches/in-furrow

canonical.summary: Brown rot infection occurs through blossom parts and progresses into the twig, killing blossoms, spurs, and associated leaves, with small cankers forming on twigs below infected spurs and beige-colored spore masses on diseased flowers under high humidity. diagnostic_features: Twigs develop elliptical cankers with profuse gumming at the margin between diseased and healthy tissue; leaves on infected shoots turn brown and wither but remain attached. treatments: Rely on good sanitation and proper timing of protectant fungicides
Prune blighted (diseased) shoots back to healthy tissue during dry weather; remove and destroy infected twigs and branches in summer
Shorten large trees and prune out shaded limbs in summer for a more open canopy that dries out quickly
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit in and around the tree; remove fallen fruit to reduce rot at harvest
Control insects that could wound and injure fruit, and avoid wounding fruit during harvest
Cool fruit rapidly after harvest; a short (2.5 min) soak in hot water (122°F) has reduced postharvest decay in nectarines and peaches
Use moderate amounts of nitrogen fertilizer
Apply fungicides during the bloom period at early popcorn, full bloom, and/or petal fall to control the blossom blight phase; fruit-rot sprays can be applied before harvest if wet weather is expected
Start treatment at the popcorn stage of bloom and spray every 14 days until bloom is completed; shorten to 10 days under heavy rainfall
Alternate or tank-mix fungicides from different FRAC groups with different modes of action to reduce resistance
Biological control options include Botector, BotryStop, Howler Evo, Serenade OPTI, and Serenade Garden Disease Control Concentrate

canonical.summary: Soft rot first appears as small, tannish, water-soaked spots that rapidly enlarge into soft, blister-like areas oozing a slimy or watery fluid; tissue is first white to cream then turns brown to black and becomes foul smelling. Foliage is chlorotic with leaflet margins curled upward, and stems rot and become mushy.
diagnostic_features: Infected tissues are sharply delineated from healthy tissue by dark brown or black margins; decay is at first nearly odorless but develops a strong foul odor as secondary organisms invade, progressing to a chalky-white, foul-smelling mass; stem lesions are light brown but not black.
treatments: Use high quality / clean seed.
Split applications of water-soluble calcium at 100 to 200 pounds per acre during bulking to reduce soft rot infection and severity.
Harvest mature tubers with low pulp temperature and well-set skins, and avoid mechanical injury; delay harvest until skin has set (leave at least seven days after vines are dead) to reduce bruising.
Avoid excessive soil moisture before harvest to reduce lenticel infection; use clean water to wash potatoes and avoid water films on tuber surfaces during storage.
Properly suberize/cure potatoes; postharvest curing and storage temperatures are critical to soft rot management.
Eliminate as much soil as possible before storage; if harvesting wet potatoes, ventilate continually until dry.

canonical.summary: White, powdery fungal growth develops on both leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems, usually first on crown leaves, shaded lower leaves and leaf undersurfaces. diagnostic_features: The first sign is pale yellow leaf spots, followed by white powdery spots (asexual conidia) on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles and stems; late in the season, dark brown chasmothecia about 0.003 inches in diameter develop and are barely discernable without a hand lens.
treatments: Plant varieties with complete or partial resistance/tolerance to powdery mildew; when possible select varieties with homozygous resistance (from both parents).
Provide good air movement around plants through proper spacing, staking, and weed control; avoid planting too dense of stands and locations shaded by tall plants or structures.
Apply fertilizer based on soil test results and avoid over-applying nitrogen.
Rotate at least 2 years out of cucurbits, and physically separate or plant up-wind of older cucurbit plantings that can serve as a source of conidia.
Remove debris, weeds, and volunteers that may harbor the pathogen.
Scout regularly — examine mature/older leaves (e.g. five mature leaves at multiple field locations, or 50 older leaves) and begin fungicide applications when one leaf in 50 shows symptoms.
Apply fungicides on a 7-10 day interval beginning early in disease development, ensuring thorough coverage of leaf undersides and the lower canopy.
Alternate among fungicides with different modes of action / FRAC groups and tank-mix mobile (systemic) fungicides with a protectant (contact) fungicide to manage resistance development.
Recommended protectant fungicides include chlorothalonil (e.g. Bravo Weather Stik, Echo 720, Daconil), sulfur, copper, and mineral/horticultural oils (e.g. JMS Stylet Oil, Neem oil, Trilogy).

Targeted/mobile fungicide options include DMI/FRAC 3 (e.g. Proline, Procure, Luna Experience, Rhyme, Myclobutanil/Rally, Mettle, Tebuzol, Topguard), Quinoxyfen (Quintec, FRAC 13), Metrafenone (Vivando, FRAC 50/U8), Cyflufenamid (Torino, FRAC U6), strobilurins/FRAC 11 (e.g. Azoxystrobin, Pyraclostrobin), Fontelis (FRAC 7), OSO (FRAC 19), and premixes such as Pristine, Quadris Top, Aprovia Top, Inspire Super, Merivon, Miravis Prime.

For organic production use OMRI-approved options — the only OMRI-labeled active ingredients with some efficacy are fixed copper formulations, along with bicarbonates (Carb-O-Nator, Kaligreen, MilStop SP), oils, and biopesticides (botanical oils, hydrogen dioxide, microbes; e.g. Regalia, Serenade Opti, Double Nickel, Actinovate AG).
For home gardeners, use products containing copper or chlorothalonil ('Daconil') and grow varieties with tolerance.

canonical.summary: Aboveground symptoms include uneven stands, weak shoot growth, aerial tubers, necrosis at sprout tips, and yellowing, purpling/chlorotic, upward-curling leaves. On belowground stems and stolons it causes reddish-brown lesions that develop into sunken cankers; stolons and stems can be girdled, producing a pruning effect and stunting. Black scurf — an accumulation of irregular black sclerotia (sclerotized mycelium) — forms on the tuber surface, and affected tubers are deformed.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-brown lesions on belowground stems and stolons that develop into sunken cankers, girdling of stolons causing a pruning effect, and accumulation of irregular black sclerotia (black scurf) on the tuber surface that are not easily removed and do not affect the tuber interior — giving rise to the name "the dirt that doesn't wash off" — especially visible on fresh-market red and white-skinned varieties.

treatments: Plant certified seed tubers free from sclerotia; if more than 20 sclerotia are visible on one side of washed tubers, consider a different seed source
Treat all seed — fungicide treatment of seed pieces (or treat with antagonists/fungicides if seed is not certified) reduces seedborne inoculum
Apply fungicides to seed pieces and/or in-furrow at planting to reduce disease on belowground stems and stolons; post-planting applications can reduce tuber blemish on daughter tubers
Practice long rotations (2-3+ years out of potatoes; rotations with canola, barley, or sweet corn) to reduce soilborne inoculum; avoid two consecutive potato seasons on the same land
Favor rapid emergence — warm seed tubers before planting, plant at shallow depth (cover with no more than two inches of soil), avoid early/cold-wet planting, and avoid overwatering
Harvest quickly after vine desiccation / as soon as the skin is set to limit black scurf and bruising
Remove or burn vines to reduce overwintering fungus, and separate tubers from crop residues after stem destruction
Increase crop-residue decomposition and soil organic matter; chisel plowing reduces incidence and severity
Conduct a soil test for nutrients and pH (low pH is not conducive to disease)
Use disease-free soil, avoid fields with a history of potato production or black scurf/stem canker, and do not dump infested tubers on future potato fields
Plant less susceptible cultivars

On belowground stems and stolons it causes reddish-brown lesions that develop into sunken cankers; stolons and stems can be girdled, producing a pruning effect and stunting. Black scurf — an accumulation of irregular black sclerotia (sclerotized mycelium) — forms on the tuber surface, and affected tubers are deformed.

On belowground stems and stolons, Rhizoctonia solani typically causes reddish-brown lesions that often develop into sunken cankers... they often develop black scurf , an accumulation of irregular black sclerotia of R. solani on the tuber surface.

diagnostic_features.quote: Rhizoctonia solani typically causes reddish-brown lesions that often develop into sunken cankers. diagnostic_features: Reddish, thickened, puckered leaf areas causing curling, turning pale yellow then grayish white (powdery) from spore production; can also cause stunted, thickened, distorted shoots and rare corky, cracked fruit.
treatments: Plant resistant/tolerant cultivars (e.g. Frost, Indian Free, Muir, Q-1-8, Avalon, Mary Jane for peaches; Kreibich for nectarines; Redhaven tolerant)
Apply a preventive fungicide every year after leaves fall but before new buds develop in spring; a single well-timed dormant spray can control the disease
Effective dormant-season fungicides include copper products (copper soap/copper octanoate, fixed copper, Bordeaux mixture), chlorothalonil, liquid lime sulfur, and Ziram
Add 1% horticultural oil to copper sprays to increase effectiveness
Time application when ~90% of leaves have fallen (late Nov–Dec); add a second application in late winter before buds swell in high-rainfall/wet areas
Thoroughly cover all branches and twigs to the point of runoff (until dripping)
Prune in fall prior to fungicide application to reduce overwintering spore numbers
Maintain tree vigor (extra fruit thinning, irrigation to reduce drought stress, extra nitrogen) and follow IPM practices

treatments: Manage primarily with fungicide treatments to protect buds and twigs from infection
Prune out and destroy infected wood (dormant-season pruning is very effective)
Angle sprinkler heads low enough to keep from wetting the canopy
Bordeaux mixture and some copper formulations are acceptable for organically certified orchards
Spray at leaf fall (Nov 15 - Dec 1, before winter rains) to protect against twig infections
Apply during bloom / at shuck fall to prevent fruit and leaf infection, repeating about two weeks later
Apply again later in summer (fruit softening) only if a 4-hour rain is forecast

Residential products: myclobutanil (Spectracide Immunox, Monterey Fungimax, Fertilome F-stop), captan, or Natural Guard Copper Soap (organic)

canonical.summary: Symptoms appear first on the oldest foliage as circular to angular dark brown lesions 3–4 mm in diameter, often with concentric rings producing a target-board (bulls-eye) effect; severely infected leaves turn yellow and drop, and infected tubers show a brown, corky dry rot.
diagnostic_features: The bulls-eye (concentric ring / target-board) pattern of lesions on leaves and stems, often infecting the oldest leaves first and progressing upward.
treatments: Use only clean seed saved from disease-free plants / certified seed potatoes.
At the end of the season, remove and destroy crop residue; where not practical, plow residue into the soil to promote breakdown and remove the spore source from the soil surface.
Practice crop rotation to non-susceptible crops such as small grains or brassica crops for three years.
Control volunteer plants that emerge from the previous year's planting.
Maintain good weed management, especially of susceptible weeds such as hairy nightshade or black nightshade.
Promote good air circulation by proper spacing of plants; orient rows toward prevailing winds, avoid shaded areas and wind barriers.
Irrigate early in the day to promote rapid drying of foliage, and use drip irrigation where possible to keep foliage dry.
When pruning lower tomato leaves, clean the cutting tool with 70% rubbing alcohol to limit spread.
Provide proper fertilization and mineral balance, and maintain optimum growing conditions.
Minimize plant injury and the spread of spores by controlling insect feeding.
Hand-pick diseased foliage in small fields to slow spread (not a sole control).
Do not work in a wet garden/field.

Use resistant or tolerant varieties (e.g. tomato: Mountain Magic, Juliet, Defiant PhR, Verona, Jasper; potato: Russet Burbank, Lamoka, Snowden, Lehigh, Ranger Russet, Elba with moderate resistance); check seed for the "EB" resistance designation.
Grow later maturing, longer season varieties.
Apply fungicides only when justified by early disease initiation; when justified, apply as soon as symptoms appear with continued protection at 7- to 10-day intervals.

Fungicides available include chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin (Quadris), boscalid (Endura), famoxadone/cymoxanil (Tanos), fenamidone (Reason 500SC), iprodione (Rovral 4F), and pyraclostrobin (Headline).

canonical.summary: Symptoms most commonly appear as wilting or dieback of a branch or branches on an otherwise healthy-appearing tree or shrub; beneath the bark the wood is discolored brown to reddish-brown instead of white, and cankers may appear sunken, darkened, blistered, or have peeling bark.
diagnostic_features: If bark is removed, the wood beneath the bark will be discolored brown to reddish-brown instead of white; on gum-producing trees gum may exude from cankered areas (gummosis); black fungal spore-producing structures (pycnidia) are sometimes present and are white inside when sliced open.
treatments: Ensure plants are in optimal health by providing appropriate cultural requirements, avoiding plant stress and injury, and employing appropriate sanitation measures.
Use proper plant selection and placement in the landscape; select plants with an appropriate hardiness zone rating for the region.
Provide irrigation to trees and shrubs during dry periods.
Protect susceptible trees and shrubs from a sudden and significant drop in temperature when possible.
Avoid planting locations compacted by construction or foot traffic and soils that are excessively wet or drain poorly.
Practice proper pruning techniques to avoid large pruning wounds.
Prune out dead wood, cutting back to a healthy area on the branch (white to cream-colored inside when cut), because Botryosphaeria spp. colonize dead wood and can move into healthy wood.
Disinfect pruning tools with rubbing alcohol between cuts to prevent spreading inoculum.
Place mulch no more than 2 inches deep over the root zone, keeping it from contacting the bark of woody plants.

canonical.summary: Infected leaves develop roughly circular or irregularly shaped black spots up to 1/2 inch (about 2-12 mm) in diameter with feathery/fringed margins, usually on the upper leaf surface; affected leaves yellow and drop, and the disease progresses up the canes until the entire plant defoliates. Canes may develop raised purplish-red blotches that blacken and blister.
diagnostic_features: Black spots up to 1/2 inch in diameter with fringed/feathery borders on the upper leaf surface; close inspection reveals acervuli (black spore-bearing structures) producing two-celled spores (conidia) and white, slimy masses of conidia.
treatments: Plant rose cultivars with resistance to black spot
Sanitation: rake and remove/discard fallen leaves and prune and discard infected canes
Promote good air circulation: space plants far apart, plant in open sunny high-light locations, avoid dense plantings
Avoid wetting foliage; water at the base with soaker/drip hose and avoid overhead irrigation; restrict irrigation during cloudy, humid weather
Disinfest pruning tools between cuts (e.g., 70% alcohol for at least 30 seconds or a 10% bleach solution); prune only in dry weather
Apply labeled protectant fungicides every 7-14 days from bud break/spring leaf emergence through the season; spray before rain to protect leaves

Effective active ingredients include chlorothalonil, copper (copper sulfate/copper products), myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin, mancozeb/maneb, thiophanate-methyl, captan, propiconazole, and triforine; organic options include neem oil, sulfur, lime sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, and hydrogen dioxide
Rotate/alternate at least two active ingredients with different modes of action to minimize fungicide resistance

canonical.summary: In peach and nectarine, symptoms include delays in leaf emergence, flowering and fruit maturity, bud necrosis or doubling, leaf mottling and deformation, and fruit deformation. canonical.summary: Brown spots appear on leaves which enlarge and coalesce, developing concentric lighter/darker brown rings; infected leaves turn tan to bronze and drop, causing total leaf loss (extensive defoliation) within days. Black streaks or sunken lesions form on stems from the top to the soil line, leading to branch dieback, and plants often die shortly after all leaves drop.
diagnostic_features: Concentric lines of darker and lighter shades of brown develop as leaf spots enlarge; black streaks or lesions occur on stems from the top to the soil line and dark brown to black sunken areas form anywhere on stems; root infection does not occur; under warm, humid conditions white crystalline/quartz-like spore masses form on leaf undersides and in stem lesions; total leaf loss can occur within days of first symptoms.
treatments: Plant only disease-free new boxwood and host plants, buying from local, reputable suppliers who have thoroughly inspected the plants; purchase plants free of any leaf spots or stem lesions.
Quarantine/isolate new boxwood away from established plants for at least one month (several weeks) to observe for symptoms before planting.
If symptoms are noticed, have the plant(s) checked at a plant diagnostic laboratory.

If boxwood blight is confirmed, remove and destroy affected shrubs (roots and all), plus fallen leaves and branches and plants within 10 feet, by burning (where allowed), deep burying (at least two feet), or double bagging and landfilling.
Do NOT compost any parts of infected shrubs.
Thoroughly decontaminate any tools used in removal by treating them for at least 30 seconds in 70% alcohol or, as a last resort, 10% bleach.
Choose boxwood blight-resistant varieties where possible.
Do not plant boxwoods where boxwood blight has been a problem in the past, and replant removed sites with non-host plants.
Space boxwood plants far enough apart that branches of adjacent shrubs do not overlap.
Avoid overhead/sprinkler watering; use a soaker or drip hose.
Avoid holiday decorations that contain boxwood whenever possible.

Apply protective fungicides before symptoms develop; active ingredients include chlorothalonil (alone or combined with thiophanate-methyl or tebuconazole), fludioxonil, metconazole, tebuconazole, and mancozeb, with thorough coverage to runoff.
When using fungicides, treat every 7 to 14 days throughout the growing season and alternate active ingredients (except do not alternate metconazole and tebuconazole, which are chemically related).
Routinely (e.g., weekly) check boxwood plants for boxwood blight.

canonical.summary: Before new growth appears in spring, infected shoots fail to flush; leaves on the tips of infected branches turn red, then bronze/brown and finally tan or yellowish, bend upwards and lay close to their stems while remaining attached, and infected branches die back. In moist weather the fungus produces salmon-pink to orange fruiting bodies on leaves and stems.
diagnostic_features: During wet/high-humidity events the fungus produces salmon-pink to sticky orange spore masses (sporodochia), viewable with a hand lens, on the lower surface of infected leaves and on cankered stems; this distinguishes Volutella blight from winter injury and Boxwood blight. Affected branches show loose bark, girdling, and wood discoloration, and dead leaves remain attached and bend upward.
treatments: Prune out diseased branches several inches below the transition zone, in dry weather and with sharp, sanitized tools.
Thin (rather than shear) boxwood to improve air circulation and light penetration; remove dense inner stems and crowding plants.
Sanitize pruning tools after each plant by wiping clean and dipping/spraying with 10% bleach, 70% isopropyl alcohol, or a commercial disinfectant.
Shake out and rake up old, fallen, and diseased leaves (including those lodged in branch crotches) and dispose of them away from boxwoods.
Dig out and destroy severely infected plants.
Improve growing conditions and provide adequate irrigation during the dry season to alleviate drought stress; avoid excess watering, soggy soil, and excess fertilization.
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or flood irrigation and direct hand watering to the soil while keeping foliage dry.
Establish new plants in well-drained soil, do not overcrowd, and provide proper nutrition based on soil test results.
Do not remove more than one-third of the healthy branches in a single year; make cuts just outside the branch collar and bark ridge to minimize wounding.

Apply preventive fungicides (Bordeaux mixture or other copper fungicide, chlorothalonil, or mancozeb) in late winter/early spring before new growth emerges, continuing every 7 to 10 days until new growth is complete.

canonical.summary: Tomato leaves develop small (less than 1/8 inch), brown, circular spots surrounded by a yellow halo, with centers that often fall out leaving small holes; pepper leaf spots lack a yellow halo. Spots are dark brown to black, rarely more than 3 mm; fruit spots are slightly raised, brown and scabby.
diagnostic_features: When Xanthomonas is present, bacteria ooze (bacterial streaming) from infected tissue and can be observed under a light microscope; bacterial streaming is not seen in lesions caused by fungal pathogens. Bacterial spot leaf spots do not contain concentric rings (concentric rings suggest early blight).
treatments: Use pathogen-free certified seeds and disease-free transplants to prevent introduction into greenhouses and field production areas.
Inspect transplants carefully and reject any with spots or discoloration, including your own.
Treat seeds to kill bacteria on and in seed (hot water treatment, or dilute bleach or hydrochloric acid).
Plant resistant varieties of bell pepper, hot pepper, and tomato.
Rotate to a non-solanaceous crop and avoid fields planted with peppers or tomatoes within the past 1 (NC State) to 3-4 (UMN) years, especially where bacterial spot occurred previously.
Eliminate solanaceous weeds in and around production areas and control volunteers.
Keep foliage dry: water at the base with drip irrigation or a soaker hose in the morning; avoid overhead watering.
Do not spray, tie, harvest, work in, or handle plants when wet; avoid high-pressure sprays.
Space plants for airflow (18-24 in for caged tomatoes to 30-36 in for uncaged determinate tomatoes) and stake or cage plants.
Remove leaves with symptoms.
Bury or remove crop debris/residue at the end of the season.
Disinfect greenhouses, benches, trays, tools, and equipment between seedling crops with a commercial sanitizer (e.g., a 1:9 dilution of germicidal bleach).
In the greenhouse, discard trays adjacent to an outbreak location to minimize spread.
Keep cull piles away from field operations.
Apply labeled bactericides/fungicides preventatively: copper-based compounds, mancozeb + copper hydroxide, streptomycin sulfate (greenhouse use), bacteriophage, acibenzolar-S-methyl.
Organic options: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain MBI 600, Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713, Bacillus mycoides isolate J, copper, methyl salicylate + Bacillus thuringiensis.

canonical.summary: Early leaf spots are tan colored and expand to 1-3mm in diameter; adjacent spots may coalesce into irregular lesions, and as the disease develops, velvety dark green-brown sporulation develops within the lesions.
diagnostic_features: The presence of dark green sporulation distinguishes Cladosporium leaf spot from anthracnose and Stemphylium leaf spot, both of which also form circular lesions.
treatments: Treatment is rarely necessary.
Till under crop residues promptly after harvest to speed up decomposition; crop rotation helps reduce disease severity since the pathogen survives in crop residue.
Use seed tested for Cladosporium and other pathogens; hot water seed treatment can effectively eliminate Cladosporium from spinach seed.
Chlorine (bleach) seed treatment: soak seed for 10 minutes in a 1.2% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution; effectively eliminates the pathogen without reducing germination.
Use drip irrigation, or overhead irrigate early in the day on sunny days so foliage dries quickly; overhead irrigation may increase disease severity.
Control weeds within the crop and around the outside edge of high tunnels to increase air flow and eliminate weed hosts.

QoI fungicides (strobilurins, FRAC Group 11) effectively control the disease — labeled products for spinach include Quadris, Reason, and Cabrio, plus combination products Merivon (groups 7 & 11) and Tanos (groups 27 & 11).
Tank mix with, or use a combination product containing, a contact fungicide (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb, sulfur, oil).

Copper products are effective protectants; apply as a protectant spray at 10–14 day intervals (e.g. copper hydroxide at label rates), with a suitable agricultural spray oil for some copper formulations.
Adding a Bacillus subtilis (e.g. Serenade) or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens (e.g. Double Nickel, Stargus, Taegro, Triathlon) product to copper has a synergistic effect for better control.
Hydrogen dioxide products (e.g. OxiDate) will kill spores on contact.
The Northeast Vegetable Guide lists Lifegard at first true leaf stage or after thinning.

canonical.summary: The pathogen causes seedling damping-off, leaf spots, foliar blight, root and crown rot, stem lesions, and fruit rot; affected tissue initially appears water-soaked, turns brown, and often collapses, frequently with a white, yeast-like growth of sporangia.
diagnostic_features: A white, yeast-like growth made up mostly of lemon-shaped sporangia of Phytophthora capsici; seeing the sporangia is diagnostic.
treatments: Use long rotations between susceptible crops and select fields where Phytophthora blight has never occurred.

Select well-drained fields and manage soil moisture to avoid saturated conditions; minimize hardpans/plowpans by subsoiling or chisel plowing, subsoil between rows, and prepare raised dome-shaped beds covered with plastic mulch.
Physically separate plantings of susceptible crops (cucurbits, pepper, eggplant, and tomato) and grow a mustard biofumigant cover crop beforehand.

Avoid over-irrigating; do not irrigate at night when temperatures are above 70°F, lay drip tape a few inches from crowns, and do not irrigate from a pond that could contain water drained from an infested field.

Manage fungicide resistance using a diversity of chemistry (by FRAC code) in alternation and combination; use fungicides with targeted activity for P. capsici and oomycetes plus labeled biopesticides in a preventive program.
Scout fields routinely, especially after major rain storms, and disk localized symptomatic areas.
Clean farm equipment, shoes, etc. of soil between fields; do not discard cull fruit in the field and remove healthy-looking fruit from infested fields promptly.
Do not display pumpkin fruit for sale, or save seed, from a field where Phytophthora blight occurred; when growing small-fruited pumpkins select hard, gourd-like rinded varieties.

canonical.summary: Rotting, mushy squash, pumpkins, eggplant, or chili peppers; it first appears on dying blossoms attached to fruits, then spreads to the fruit, where affected parts turn dark brown to black and become fuzzy and mushy.
diagnostic_features: Thousands of tiny black dots can be seen with a hand lens on infected fruit, resembling a pincushion, with a fuzzy mass of fungal fruiting bodies on shriveled fruit.
look_alikes: Rotting of small summer squash fruit from poor pollination
treatments: Promptly remove and destroy infected fruit and diseased plant material during the growing season
Space plants far enough apart to provide air movement so fruit, leaves, and flowers dry quickly after rain and dew
Use physical barriers such as mulch (shredded leaves, dried grass clippings, newspaper covered with straw, plastic or paper) to prevent fruit from contacting moist soil
Use raised plant beds to reduce moisture in the lower plant canopy
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers and manage excess moisture (drainage, irrigation)
Rotate vegetables so two or more years pass before planting any member of the squash family in the same location
Remove all plant residue at the end of the growing season
Prevent wounds and avoid storing damaged and diseased fruit
Minimize post-harvest decay by refrigeration
Apply fungicides during prolonged wet periods (note: several sources report fungicides are ineffective/impractical because new susceptible flowers open daily)

summary.value: Rotting, mushy squash, pumpkins, eggplant, or chili peppers; it first appears on dying blossoms attached to fruits, then spreads to the fruit, where affected parts turn dark brown to black and become fuzzy and mushy.
summary.quote: Rotting, mushy squash, pumpkins, eggplant, or chili peppers is a symptom of a common fungal disease called choanephora rot. It first appears on dying blossoms that are still attached to fruits. The disease then spreads to the fruit (usually appears first at the blossom-end but may also appear at the stem end). Affected fruit parts turn dark brown to black and then become fuzzy and mushy.

canonical.summary: Mosaic symptoms present as blotchy or streaky patterns of yellow and green color, with broken yellow streaks running between veins on an otherwise green blade; in severe cases leaves turn necrotic and dieback can kill lawns.
diagnostic_features: Broken yellow streaks running between veins on an otherwise green blade; in the 2013 outbreak leaf symptoms included mosaic but turned necrotic and developed into severe dieback that completely killed some infected lawns.
look_alikes: St. Augustinegrass decline (SAD, caused by Panicum mosaic virus)
other turfgrass diseases with yellowed streaks
treatments: Plant host resistance is the best management tool for viral diseases
Choose a variety other than 'Floratam'; 'Palmetto', 'Bitterblue' and 'CitraBlue' may get the disease but are more resistant
Sod with SCMV should not be used; inspect sod before installing it in your lawn
Sanitize mowers and other equipment between properties: remove clippings and plant material, then spray equipment and shoes with dilute bleach, quaternary ammonia (Green-Shield), or alcohol
When mowing multiple lawns where the virus is known to occur, mow apparently healthy lawns before those with mosaic symptoms, and avoid mowing symptomatic lawns when the turfgrass canopy is wet
Maintain a healthy lawn by following best management practices, as a healthy lawn is more resistant to disease

canonical.summary: On leaves, brown to black circular spots associated with the leaf margins progress toward the center; stems develop ovate cankers near nodes that crack and exude a brown/amber gummy fluid; on fruit, circular water-soaked spots expand and may take on a black, leathery appearance (black rot).
diagnostic_features: A gummy, amber-colored exudate in the center of diseased spots and from cracked stem cankers near nodes; spots become covered with white mycelium and tiny black fungal fruiting structures (pycnidia, perithecia, pseudothecia) that swell and release tendrils of spores when wetted.
treatments: Use pathogen-free seed; purchase seeds or seedlings free of pathogens from a reputable company; if saving seed, do not collect seed from infected plants
Consider seed treatments; disinfectants as solutions are more effective than dry-dust treatments
Inspect transplant seedlings regularly and dispose of all seedlings near infected plants; avoid using healthy-looking seedlings from trays with infected plants
Rotate out of cucurbits for at least 2 years (2-4 years; two- to three-year rotation with non-hosts such as small grain or corn)
Deep plow / disk infected crop debris post-harvest to speed complete decomposition
Carefully remove all volunteers of related species; eradicate wild citrons, balsam pear, or volunteer cucurbits before planting
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation or water at the base of the stem
Remove and destroy infected fruit and vines at the end of the season in small gardens
Avoid injuring fruit during harvest; store only perfectly healthy fruit
After harvest, cure squash 2 weeks at 75°F to 85°F and store slightly below 50°F (store fruit at 45°F–50°F to prevent postharvest black rot)
Plant resistant varieties where available (resistant watermelon, pumpkin, buttercup, and canary melons available; note: NCSU states no resistant cucurbit varieties exist)
Use integrated pest management to control cucumber beetles, other insect pests, and powdery mildew

Apply fungicides preventatively; Chlorothalonil and Mancozeb are effective contact fungicides, plus many effective systemic fungicides; always alternate chemistries/modes of action to manage resistance

Registered fungicide groups include Carboxamide (Group 7: Endura, Fontelis), Chlorothalonil (Group M5: Bravo Ultrex, Echo 720, Bonide Fung-onil), Copper (Group M1, not as stand-alone), DMI (Group 3: Proline, Rhyme, Topguard), Group 29 (Omega 500F), Group 19 (OSO 5% SC), Group P5 biofungicide (Regalia), Strobilurin (Group 11: Cabrio, Evito, Quadris), Group 1 (Topsin M); premixes and biological controls (Double Nickel LC, LifeGard WG) per PNW handbook
Commercial growers should refer to the Midwest Vegetable Production Guide for specific fungicide recommendations

canonical.summary: Infection causes small, brown, irregularly shaped blotches in petals that enlarge rapidly until the entire flower is brown and dead; blighted petals are dry or leathery but do not crumble, and prominent dark brown veins give infected petals a netted appearance.
diagnostic_features: Symptoms that distinguish camellia petal blight include petal veins darker than the surrounding tissue, infections beginning near the central part of the flower (not appearing first near petal margins), and symptoms that occur only on petals.
look_alikes: injury due to chemicals, rough handling, or wind
treatments: Prevention is the best control; use fungicides only in conjunction with recommended sanitation and cultural practices.

Carefully remove and destroy diseased and spent camellia flowers, including spent flowers up in the canopy; pull off infected flowers as they appear and collect fallen blossoms, disposing of them in a covered location away from camellias.
Rake and destroy old leaves, flowers, and other plant debris, especially under the camellias.
Do not put diseased flowers on the compost heap unless they are buried; do not add camellia petals or leaves to mulch used around camellia even if composted.

Remove the top layer of potting soil when new plants are purchased and replace it with pathogen-free soil; carefully remove the top 3 to 4 inches of soil from beneath plants to eliminate sclerotia in heavily infested soil.
Plant camellias in a well-ventilated location and avoid overhead irrigation.

Each year when blossoms are no longer present, apply a fresh layer of pathogen-free organic mulch and maintain a 4-inch layer beneath and somewhat beyond plants to suppress spore production; remove fallen petals and debris before applying fresh mulch, otherwise avoid disturbing existing mulch; keep mulch thin near or several inches away from the trunk.
Use fall- or early-flowering cultivars and species (such as Camellia sasanqua) to avoid the main crop of spores in the spring.
Spray an appropriate fungicide during bloom to reduce infections, reapplying every 10 to 14 days while conditions remain suitable for the pathogen.
Bonide Captan 50 WP at 1 Tbsp/gal water (home gardens, Washington only).
Captan 80 WDG at 0.625 lb/100 gal water, applied to soil around plants when flowers begin to open; repeat at 7- to 10-day intervals during bloom (Group M4 fungicide).
Terraclor 400 at 6 to 12 fl oz/100 gal water, begin before buds open; repeat every 3 to 4 weeks during bloom (Group 14 fungicide).
Ziram 76 DF at 1.5 to 2 lb/100 gal water as a soil drench (Group M3 fungicide).
Banner MAXX at 5 to 8 fl oz/100 gal water (Group 3 fungicide).
BioAdvanced Disease Control at 0.75 fl oz/gal water.
Concert at 22 to 35 fl oz/100 gal water, landscape use only (Group 3 + M5 fungicide).
Daconil Weather Stik at 1.38 pints/100 gal water (Group M5 fungicide).
Mancozeb-based products such as Fore 80WP Rainshield or Protect DF (Group M3 fungicides).
Monsoon Turf at 4 to 10 fl oz/100 gal water (Group 3 fungicide).
Spectro 90 WDG at 1 to 2 lb/100 gal water (Group 1 + M5 fungicide).
Tebuzol 3.6F at 4 to 10 fl oz/100 gal water (Group 3 fungicide).
Torque at 4 to 10 fl oz/100 gal water/A (Group 3 fungicide).

canonical.summary: Foliar symptoms include stunting, wilting and yellowing/chlorosis with an erect, upright posture; root symptoms include a constricted taproot with a proliferation of small feeder roots (bearding) after early infection and a "wineglass" shape after late infection, with necrosis of vascular elements visible in cross-section.
diagnostic_features: A constricted taproot with proliferation of small feeder roots (bearding) after early infection, and a "wineglass" shape when infection occurs late; necrosis of vascular elements in cross-section. No interveinal chlorosis or leaf scorching is observed, distinguishing it from nitrogen deficiency, Aphanomyces root rot, and Fusarium yellows/root rot.
treatments: Use of resistant cultivars/varieties — the most effective and least expensive tool for managing this disease
Plant varieties with multi-source rhizomania resistance adapted to the growing region to minimize increase in soil inoculum
Plant resistant varieties on a minimum 4-year rotation
Plant early into cool soils
Avoid overuse of irrigation and avoid soil moisture wetter than -40 centibars
Crop rotation
Clean anything that moves soil (farm equipment, people, irrigation water, tare dirt, livestock)
Maintain good weed control in rotation crops
Prevent soil compaction and maintain good drainage
Soil fumigation and/or solarization where allowed or cost-effective
Cultural practices aimed at interfering with the vector's life cycle

canonical.summary: Browning, stunting, and twisting of new shoots and needles, with a brown discoloration beginning at the base of needles and growing toward the tip; needles die at one half to three fourths normal length, and small black fruiting bodies appear at the base of needles. Resinous cankers may appear on stems.
diagnostic_features: Fruiting bodies (pycnidia) appear as black dots at the base of the needles, often found under the needle sheaths and also on cone scales and shoots; lower branches tend to be more severely infected.
treatments: Promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries.
Do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers on pines.
Treat the entire crown of the tree, but especially the lower branches, with a fungicide as the buds begin to swell during bud break and again 2 weeks later.
Do not plant healthy 2 or 3-needled pines near older infected pines.
If infected branches are pruned out, disinfest the pruning tools between cuts.
Maintain the health of the tree by avoiding improper planting site selection and water during droughts when plants are young.
Collect all fallen cones and dispose of them to limit the spread of the disease.
Avoid planting too close to other plants that can limit airflow.
Prune diseased branches to limit the spread of the disease.
Avoid pruning during wet weather and sanitize pruning shears with 70% rubbing alcohol between cuts to minimize spreading the disease.
Appropriate Fungicides: Azoxystrobin (Quadris, Amistar, Cabrio EG), Bordeaux mix, Propiconazole (Banner Maxx), Thiophanate-methyl (Topsin-M)
Control of the disease requires that all affected twigs and cones be removed.
Fertilize trees stunted by the disease to stimulate growth.

Fungicide sprays are recommended in conjunction with cultural controls. Spray three times: 1) when buds begin to elongate/swell, 2) just before new needles begin to emerge from the fascicle sheath, and 3) 10-14 days later.
Take care to avoid wounding trees, and do not prune or shear in wet weather when spores are being released.
Mulch and water as needed to reduce stress.
Consider avoiding the use of the most susceptible pines in landscape plantings.

treatments.quote: Promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries. Do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers on pines. Treat the entire crown of the tree, but especially the lower branches, with a fungicide as the buds begin to swell during bud break and again 2 weeks later. Sprays at other times are not effective. Do not plant healthy 2 or 3-needled pines near older infected pines. If infected branches are pruned out, disinfest the pruning tools between cuts.

canonical.summary: Irregular brown spots with purplish edges on the upper leaf surface and a lighter brown spot on the lower surface; spots may merge into larger brown dead areas (blight) that can cover the entire leaf.
diagnostic_features: Irregular brown spots with purplish edges on the upper leaf surface, with a corresponding lighter brown spot on the lower surface; spots are small and circular and can coalesce into large necrotic blotches, with tiny black pycnidia forming in the necrotic tissue.
treatments: Follow good sanitation practices.
On evergreens like rhododendron and holly, prune out foliage damaged by winter injury by early spring to reduce opportunistic colonization.
On deciduous hosts like hydrangea and witchhazel, prune out badly infected leaves from the canopy and remove all prematurely shed foliage during the early growing season.
Prune to improve air flow and reduce the volume of foliage in deep shade within the interior canopy to help reduce disease severity.
Apply fungicides early in the season as new leaves are developing: copper salts of fatty and/or rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole and propiconazole.
Avoid fungicide application during periods of bloom when pollinating insects may have contact.

canonical.summary: Lesions and cankers appear on all aboveground parts of the peony; stem cankers are elongate and gray and often cause severe twisting or curling of the stem, while foliar leaf spots and flower/bud infections are gray and can cause irregular growth or interfere with flower development.
diagnostic_features: Elongate gray stem cankers that often cause severe twisting or curling of the stem, with pink-colored fruiting structures (acervulus) sometimes visible in the cankers.
treatments: Increase air movement by wide plant spacing to avoid overcrowding of plants.
Avoid overhead irrigation that keeps plants wet for extended periods of time.
Remove all infected plant parts during the growing season.
Cut and remove or destroy all plants at the end of the year to reduce overwintering inoculum.
CuPRO 5000 at 1.5 to 2 lb/A. Group M1 fungicide. 48-hr reentry.
Mancozeb-based products can be used to provide some protection. Group M3 fungicides. 24-hr reentry.
Fore 80WP Rainshield at 1.5 lb/100 gal water plus a spreader-sticker.
Protect DF at 1 to 2 lb/100 gal water plus 2 to 4 oz spreader-sticker.
Monterey Liqui-Cop at 3 Tbsp/gal water.
Nu-Cop 50 DF at 1 lb/100 gal water. Group M1 fungicide. 48-hr reentry.
Ortho Rose & Flower Disease Control at 2 fl oz/gal water. Group 3 fungicide.
Pageant at 6 to 12 oz/100 gal water. Do not use with organosilicone-based adjuvants. Group 7 + 11 fungicide. 12-hr reentry.

canonical.summary: Symptoms include rapid elongation of new shoots followed by witches' brooms (clustering of small branches), small distorted leaves that may show red pigmentation, and excessive growth of soft pliable red or green thorns on canes.
diagnostic_features: Canes develop excessive growth of unusually soft and pliable red or green thorns that may stiffen later; when this symptom is present, it is diagnostic for RRD. On RRD-diseased plants the reddish leaf color does not go away, whereas on healthy plants it usually disappears as the leaf matures.
treatments: Remove and destroy suspect roses immediately, or monitor and remove as soon as presence of RRV is ascertained
Burning diseased plants where permitted; otherwise bag and remove
Eliminate R. multiflora plants from the immediate vicinity (100-meter radius) of rose nurseries and gardens and monitor/remove any regrowth
Avoid planting cultivated roses downwind of known multiflora rose plantings
Space plants so that canes and leaves do not touch each other
Consider mixed plantings (roses with non-rose plants) to mitigate spread
Avoid using leaf blowers near roses
Promote plant health and vigor by irrigating during drought, maintaining fertility, and controlling other diseases
Control mites with certain miticides (e.g. abamectin registered for both eriophyid and spider mites); carbaryl or bifenthrin have given reasonable control
Focus miticide sprays on roses surrounding spots where RRD-diseased roses were removed; spray every two weeks from April until September, with additional sprays during hot, dry weather
