canonical.summary: Symptoms begin as small water-soaked spots on emerging shoots, stems, petioles, buds, or leaves that become dark brown to black, leathery, elongated lesions; a wet rot of crowns and roots causes collapse and death of the entire plant.
diagnostic_features: Spots become dark brown to black, leathery, elongated lesions, with a wet rot of infected crowns and roots.
treatments: Once symptoms are noticed, chemical treatments are usually not effective.
Remove all parts of the infected plant and the immediate soil from the planting.
Do not replant peonies in that location until drainage issues are resolved and infested soil has been replaced.
Do not overwater plants.
Improve drainage in areas where standing water occurs; raised beds promote drainage and reduce disease.
Inspect plants (above and below ground parts) and ensure they look healthy before purchasing or accepting them.
Implement proper sanitation practices for tools, equipment, benches, and floors; a sanitizer may be used in areas with a history of Phytophthora.
Increase organic matter in the soil.
Plant Phytophthora resistant or tolerant hosts in areas with a history of the disease.
Soil solarization of infested landscape beds may reduce the amount of pathogen in the soil; infested soil may be removed and replaced with clean soil.
Use a preventative fungicide spray program after cultural practices are implemented, alternating products with different FRAC numbers to avoid resistance.

Practice fungicide resistance management by rotating/alternating fungicides and tank-mixing across different FRAC groups

canonical.summary: Small, deep purple spots appear on the upper surface of leaves, enlarging to 0.125 to 0.25 inch (3-6 mm) with the center turning brown then gray to white; numerous spots may coalesce to kill the leaf.
diagnostic_features: On older leaves the center of the lesion changes from tan or gray to white, with reddish purple to rusty brown margins, while on younger leaves the lesions stay light brown.
treatments: Use disease-free plants and certified, disease-free nursery stock; cull severely infected plants.
Plant resistant cultivars (e.g. 'Crimson King', 'Earliglow', 'Glooscap', 'Ogallala', 'Ozark Beauty').
Plant in full sunlight, in well-drained soils, with proper spacing to optimize air circulation.
Use drip irrigation or a soaker hose; avoid overhead watering (do not use a sprinkler).
Do not work in the strawberry patch when it is wet; wait until the patch is dry.
Remove infected leaves when practical and reduce inoculum on planting stock.
For June-bearing strawberries, bed renovation techniques (in particular mowing) can be useful; at season's end remove plant debris (deep bury, burn, or hot compost).

Apply fungicides only when monitoring indicates they are necessary; products containing captan, myclobutanil, copper, or chlorothalonil. Use copper-containing fungicides only prior to flowering, and alternate myclobutanil with another active ingredient.
Soil fumigation may successfully reduce inoculum levels in the field for matted row production systems.

canonical.summary: Black knot forms characteristic black, warty, elongated knots (swellings) on the woody parts of the tree — most often on twigs and branches and sometimes trunks. The swellings first appear as inconspicuous, olive-greenish and corky growths, then become black and hard, ranging from about an inch to a foot or more in length, and may encircle the branch.
diagnostic_features: Knots progress over years: soft green to brown swellings the first year, often starting to form near the point of leaf attachment, then olive-green with a velvety texture, then rupture, darken, and harden into irregular, rough, black knots up to a foot or more long that encircle and elongate along the branch. Diseased twigs often bend due to one-sided overgrowth.
treatments: Select Prunus (plum/cherry) cultivars with high resistance to black knot where possible, and avoid known susceptible varieties (moderately resistant plums include Damson, Bluefree, Shiro, Santa Rosa, Formosa, Methley, Milton, Early Italian, Bradshaw, and Fellenberg).
Do not make new plantings of plums next to old ones with black knot.
Remove wild plum and cherry trees within at least 500 feet of desirable plants/new orchard, as they can harbor the disease.
Inspect nursery stock carefully before purchase to be sure trees are disease free.

Prune out knots and swellings during the dormant season before growth begins in spring (before April 1), cutting 3-4 inches (and up to 6-8 inches) below the knot/symptomatic tissue since the fungus grows beyond the visible swelling.

On large branches and trunks, excise/cut out the knots down to healthy wood, removing about 1 inch of clean wood around the knot; this is done most successfully in August when the fungus does not extend far beyond the visible swelling.
Disinfect/sterilize pruning tools between cuts (dip in 10% bleach or 70% rubbing alcohol).
Destroy prunings by burning, burying, or removing them from the site to prevent new infections.
Remove severely infected or very susceptible trees entirely.
A dormant spray of lime sulfur may be helpful when pruning heavily infected trees.

After knots are removed, fungicide sprays can be applied beginning at bud break/when flower buds begin to open to protect young green shoots, repeated every 7-10 days (week to two weeks, especially before rain) until shoots mature; effective fungicides include captan, chlorothalonil, fenbuconazole, propiconazole, thiabendazole, and wettable sulfur. (Note: the University of Wisconsin reports that fungicides are not recommended as they are not effective in most situations.)

canonical.summary: On mature leaves, small pale yellow, water-soaked areas emerge near veins and enlarge rapidly, turning tan to dark brown, coalescing into blighted, distorted leaves whose dry dead centers crack and tear (ragged appearance); petiole and stem lesions are elongate and slightly sunken; older fruit develop circular, noticeably sunken, dark-green to black lesions which may exhibit a salmon-colored exudate in moist weather.
diagnostic_features: Cucumber leaf spots often have a yellow halo while watermelon leaf spots are smaller and dark brown to black, and melon infections often exude a reddish gum; fruit spots may have fluffy white cotton-like mycelia and sticky salmon-colored spores during wet weather. The disease is easily diagnosed with a hand lens or microscope when whisker-like setae (hairs) can be seen in the pink spore masses.

treatments: Plant only certified disease-free seed from a reputable source; do not save seed from infected plants; consider seed treatments.
Rotate out of cucurbits for at least two to three years before replanting any member of the squash family in the same location.
Grow resistant cultivars (available for cucumber, watermelon, pickling and slicing cucumbers), keeping in mind which race is present in the area.
Control all weeds, especially volunteer cucurbits.
Provide proper plant spacing and use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers so foliage dries quickly; if overhead irrigation is needed, irrigate in early morning.
Do not work in or move machinery/workers through plants when foliage is wet; clean and sanitize tools, shoes and equipment after working in infected areas.
Collect and burn or deep/flip plow infected crop debris after harvest; in large fields till under crop residue.
Avoid wounding fruit during harvest, and immerse harvested fruit in clean fresh water containing 120 ppm chlorine.

Apply protective/eradicant fungicides with thorough coverage of upper and lower leaf surfaces and fruit, beginning at first appearance of disease and repeating every 5 to 10 days (shorter interval in rainy weather).

canonical.summary: Cherry leaf spot begins as purple spots on the upper surface of older leaves in early summer that grow to about 1/4 inch across and turn reddish-brown then brown; yellow areas form around the spots, leaves die and fall, and the spot centers often drop out leaving small holes.
diagnostic_features: Leaf spot infections often dry up and fall out of the leaves, resulting in small holes scattered across the leaf, or a "shothole" appearance; fungal spores are produced on the lower surface of leaf spots.
treatments: Keep the orchard clean — sanitation is a critical component of cherry leaf spot control.
Rake up and compost fallen cherry leaves in September or October.
Begin fungicide applications two weeks after bloom when leaves are completely unfolded, and repeat throughout the growing season at the interval on the label, including one application after harvest.
Use fungicides with an active ingredient of myclobutanil or captan to protect leaves from infection when applied properly.
To avoid fungicide resistance, alternate between myclobutanil and captan when making repeated applications.
Fungicides with an active ingredient of copper may provide some protection against leaf spot infection.
Combine fungicides with sanitation for best results.

canonical.summary: Peach scab causes small, slightly raised reddish-grey oval or circular lesions on green shoots that expand and develop dark brown borders, and sunken lesions on fruit that enlarge into large, dark, grey to olive, circular, well-defined lesions, sometimes with a yellowish halo.
diagnostic_features: Peach scab lesions are sunken (not raised), grey to olive, circular and well-defined, sometimes with a yellowish halo; the corky cell layer beneath the lesions does not expand as the fruit grows, causing cracks in the skin, and lesions are often concentrated around the stem end of the fruit.
treatments: Plan during orchard establishment with proper site selection, avoiding low-lying areas with poor air circulation and soil drainage.
Implement a monitoring program based on the presence of lesions on the bark.
Reduce inoculum sources by removing wild or neglected stone-fruit trees growing nearby.
Ensure proper pruning practices keep the tree canopy open to facilitate fungicide spray penetration.
Apply fungicide sprays just before peak infection periods to protect developing fruit; shorten spray intervals during frequent spring precipitation and rotate fungicides to avoid resistance.

Fungicide options include sulfur, chlorothalonil, captan, azoxystrobin (Abound), tebuconazole, fenbuconazole, difenoconazole plus cyprodinil, pyraclostrobin plus boscalid (Pristine), pyraclostrobin plus fluxapyroxad (Merivon), and thiophanate-methyl (Topsin-M).

summary.quote: Infection in young, green shoots commonly begins with small, slightly raised, reddish-grey oval or circular lesions approximately 0.08 in (2 mm) in diameter. As shoots mature, the lesions expand to 0.1–0.3 in. (3–8 mm) and develop dark brown borders (Figure 2).

diagnostic_features.quote: Peach scab causes sunken lesions on the skin of fruit (Figure 3). ... Older lesions are grey to olive in color, circular, and well-defined. ... a yellowish halo may surround the dark lesions in fruit with a significant blush.

canonical.summary: Reddish-orange spots appear on the needles of infected pines in early spring; pads of fungal tissue swell and rupture, releasing flattened white spore-bearing structures (aecia), and heavily infected needle tips can be blighted.
diagnostic_features: Reddish-orange dots on yellow spots or bands on needles, followed by flat-sided, white columns (aecia) that break open at the sides; because the base of the needles remains green, infected needles are often retained in the canopy; bright orange pustules (uredinia) develop on the aster host, becoming reddish brown and crusty (telia).
treatments: If the disease is a continuous problem across managed landscapes, avoid planting members of the Asteraceae (specifically asters and goldenrods) near two- and three-needle pines.
Chemical management to control rust diseases is notoriously difficult and is not recommended here.
Provide good air circulation; do not crowd plants.
Practice good weed control so lower needles are not kept moist for extended periods of time.
For high-value trees, remove and destroy fallen needles that collect in branch crotches and on the ground.
Protect trees in late summer when telia are seen on alternate hosts.

Heritage at 1 to 4 oz/100 gal water plus a non-silicone-based wetter sticker. Registered for conifers including Christmas trees. Group 11 fungicide. 4-hr reentry.

canonical.summary: Browning, stunting, and twisting of new shoots and needles, with a brown discoloration starting at the base of needles and growing toward the tip; small black fruiting bodies erupt through infected needles and on second-year cone scales, and resin oozes from shoot buds as growth begins in early spring.
diagnostic_features: Small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) of the fungus can be seen with the unaided eye at the base of needles, just under the fascicle or sheath tissue, and on the scales of two-year-old seed cones; needles die by the time they are one half to three fourths normal length, and dead needles are held on the shoots.
treatments: Apply fungicide to the entire crown (especially lower branches) beginning when buds begin to swell/elongate at bud break, again just before needles emerge from the fascicle sheath, and again 10-14 days (about 2 weeks) later; sprays at other times are not effective.
Remove all affected twigs and cones; if infected branches are pruned out, disinfest pruning tools between cuts.
Avoid wounding trees and do not prune or shear in wet weather (spring) when spores are being released.

Promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries; mulch and water as needed to reduce stress; fertilize stunted trees but do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers on pines.
Do not plant susceptible or healthy 2- or 3-needled pines near older, mature infected pines; remove old infected pines or keep seedling beds/plantings away from them.
Consider avoiding the use of the most susceptible pines in landscape plantings and follow good Integrated Pest Management practices.

canonical.summary: Fusarium dry rot appears as an internal light to dark brown or black rot of the potato tuber that is usually dry, often beginning at an injury and rotting out the center; infected seed pieces may completely decay.
diagnostic_features: The rot is dry; extensive rotting causes tissue to shrink and collapse, leaving a dark sunken area on the tuber surface and internal cavities, with yellow, white, or pink mold sometimes present; lesions appear wrinkled with white tufts of mycelium.
treatments: Purchase seed with as little dry rot as possible
Warm seed tubers to at least 50°F before handling and cutting to minimize injury
Clean and disinfect the seed storage area before receiving seed
Keep cutter knives sharp for a smooth cut that heals easily
Disinfect seed cutting and handling equipment often and clean up between seed lots
Adjust the cutter and sort to provide 2-ounce seed pieces
Grade out obviously rotted tubers before they reach the cutter
Treat seed pieces with fungicide to control decay and seedborne pathogens
Protect seed from wind and sunlight during planting
Do not precut seed; cut only as much as can be planted within 24 hours
Plant symptomatic seed in warm soil and cover with as little soil as practical
Harvest after skins are set and when pulp temperature is greater than 50°F
Use antibruise practices when harvesting and piling potatoes
Ensure adequate coverage if using a postharvest fungicide
Allow wounds to heal before dropping storage temperature
Provide good air circulation, high humidity (>90%), and temperature around 55°F
Drop storage temperature slowly to prevent condensation
Monitor storages often for dry rot
Market tubers with significant dry rot as soon as possible
Never grade tubers and return them to storage (spreads disease)
Allow tubers to mature before harvest and prevent harvest/storage damage
Plant when soil temperature is at least 45°F and soil moisture is 60-80% of field capacity
Plant seed with a pulp temperature warmer than the soil temperature
Avoid irrigation before emergence if possible
Seed treatment fungicides: fludioxonil (Maxim PSP), flutolanil/mancozeb (MonCoat MZ)
Postharvest fungicides: azoxystrobin/fludioxonil/difenoconazole (Stadium), phosphites (Phostrol)

canonical.summary: White, powdery spots develop on leaves late in the growing season, with older leaves entirely coated; leaves become chlorotic, then necrotic and fall from the plant, and severe defoliation may kill plants.
diagnostic_features: Leaf infection may show the green island effect where areas around colonies remain green while the rest of the plant tissue appears senescent (yellow).
treatments: Choose resistant/disease-resistant varieties; maculata varieties are generally more resistant than paniculata varieties (e.g., Phlox 'David', 'Franz Shubert').
Space plants for good air circulation, provide proper light levels, and move plants from shaded to sunnier areas of the landscape.
Regularly scout susceptible plants and zones; avoid overcrowding, overwatering, and poorly drained soil; eliminate weeds.
Replace overhead watering with drip or soaker irrigation; if overhead watering cannot be avoided, do it in the early morning.

Remove and dispose of infected leaves, branches, flowers, or fruits (burn or bag in a closed container); do not compost diseased material; sterilize tools between plants; remove plant debris, especially in fall, to prevent overwintering.
Begin fungicides at the first sign of powdery mildew on susceptible varieties; fungicides do best when used before symptoms develop, at 7- to 14-day intervals (shorter when conditions favor disease).
Alternate or tank-mix products from different FRAC groups with different modes of action and limit the use of any one group; periodically vary the fungicide to manage resistance.
Organic options: neem oil, copper or phosphorus fungicides, sulfur (e.g., Safer Brand Garden Fungicide II 0.4% sulfur), and bicarbonate-based products.

PNW fungicide options: Avelyo (Group 3), Broadform (7+11), Compass (11), Eagle 20 EW (3), Heritage (11), Insignia SC (11), Mural (7+11), Myclobutanil 20 EW T&O (3), Orkestra (7+11), Ortho Rose & Flower Disease Control (3), Pageant (7+11), Pipron (5, greenhouse only), Postiva (3+7), Propiconazole-based products such as Banner MAXX/Concert/Bonide Infuse (3), Seido (50), Spectracide Immunox (3), Terraguard SC (3), Tourney EZ (3), Trinity (3).
Biological control: Cease or Rhapsody (Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713) at 2 to 8 quarts/100 gal water.

Homeowner products (Arkansas): chlorothalonil products (Fertilome Broad Spectrum, Hi-Yield, Ortho Maxx, Garden Tech Daconil, Bonide Fung-onil), myclobutanil & permethrin (Spectracide Immunox Plus), tebuconazole products (Bonide Rose Rx, Bio Advanced), and thiophanate-methyl (Bonide Infuse Systemic).

canonical.summary: Roughly circular or sometimes angular ¼ to ½ inch diameter dead spots on leaves, often with a purple-red border, centers that may fall out, and a diffuse ring of black dots within the spots.
diagnostic_features: Spots often have a purple-red border, and the centers may eventually fall out; within the spots, a diffuse ring of black dots (reproductive structures of the fungus) is typically visible. Infections before full leaf expansion can cause puckering and distortion.
treatments: Remove and burn (where allowed by local ordinance), bury or hot compost fallen, infected leaves.
Thin plants to increase airflow and promote rapid drying of foliage.
Water plants at the base using a soaker or drip hose to minimize wetting of leaves and reduce the movement of spores.

Make an initial fungicide application as leaves first begin to emerge. If the weather is cool and wet, make additional applications at seven to 14 day intervals until hotter, drier weather develops or until leaves are fully expanded and mature.
Chlorothalonil, copper, mancozeb and thiophanate-methyl are labeled for Guignardia leaf spot control.
Do not use the same active ingredient for all treatments (particularly if you are using thiophanate-methyl); instead, alternate the use of at least two active ingredients.

canonical.summary: Infected shoots show no symptoms during the season they are infected; early the following spring (typically February-March) the infected foliage turns pale green to yellow, then branch tips turn brown and die, with affected twig tissues showing an ash-gray coloration covered with small black fruiting bodies.
diagnostic_features: Black pinhead-sized fruiting structures often appear at the base of dead twigs; symptoms appear earlier in the year than Phomopsis (usually February and March), and later in the spring (May-June) the affected foliage drops.
treatments: Whenever possible, plant resistant varieties; if the site is particularly conducive to Kabatina blight, replace susceptible plants with conifers better adapted to the site.
During dry weather, remove and dispose of infected plant parts to improve appearance and reduce Kabatina blight inoculum in the planting.
Promote rapid foliar drying to reduce the ability of Kabatina spores to infect; provide adequate spacing between plants for sufficient air flow.
Avoid prolonged night-time watering and overhead sprinklers; if overhead irrigation is used, water before midday so foliage dries rapidly in the afternoon.
If plants are shaded or crowded, prune adjacent plants to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration.
Protect vulnerable conifers from winter drying.

Prompt application of fungicides after wounding events, especially if conditions are wet, can protect wounded tissue from infection and reduce extensive secondary damage; however, both blights generally do not require chemical control in natural, established plantings, and fungicide use may be avoided by following good Integrated Pest Management practices.

canonical.summary: Small, yellow-to-brown, resin-soaked spots form on needles throughout the summer; needle tips die and turn brown while the base remains green, and in autumn diseased needles turn reddish-brown and fall off.
diagnostic_features: Yellow-to-brown resin-soaked spots on needles with the needle tip dead and brown but the base remaining green; tiny black pimple-like bumps (spore-producing structures) push through the surface within the spots.
treatments: Maintain good air circulation around trees.
Don't overcrowd plants. Use the mature size of the tree as a spacing guide when planting.
Remove the bottom most branches from the trunk to help increase air circulation around the tree.
Remove all weeds under the trees and maintain a 3 to 4 inch deep, even layer of wood chip mulch to prevent weed growth.
Leave at least a 2 inch space between the mulch and the trunk; do not mound mulch around the trunk.
Don't allow sprinklers to spray needles.
Prune and shear trees only when needles are dry.
If pruning infected trees, sterilize pruning equipment between trees with a 10 percent household bleach solution or a commercial disinfectant.
Apply a fungicide with copper sulfate or chlorothalonil as the active ingredient when needles are half-grown and again in 3 to 4 weeks.
Prune lower canopy and heavily diseased branches to improve air flow and light penetration, reduce lingering moisture, and reduce fungal inoculum.
Thin dense groves of eastern white pine to reduce disease severity.
Provide full sun settings for ornamental pines susceptible to infection.
Provide supplemental water for newly planted and young trees.

Fungicides with potential utility include azoxystrobin, benzovindiflupyr, copper salts of fatty and/or rosin acids, copper hydroxide, mancozeb, metconazole, phosphites, propiconazole and thiophanate-methyl.
Apply fungicide during spring and early summer to allow new needles to emerge and remain uninfected.
Soil drenching with phosphites for root uptake may provide some level of control.
Nitrogen fertilization can help trees regain nutrients lost due to premature needle shedding.

canonical.summary: Infected needles develop yellow spots in late summer to early autumn before turning yellow to brown, with symptoms first appearing at the needle tips and progressing to the base; black, football-shaped spore-bearing structures appear along the center of diseased needles.
diagnostic_features: Black, football-shaped lesions (apothecia) scattered along the center of the needle that split longitudinally to extrude a clear mass of spores when moisture is plentiful.
treatments: Prune out heavily diseased branches and remove any dead stems/branches, especially those in the lower canopy, as Lophodermium can overwinter in woody tissues.
Cover discarded needles around the base of the tree with mulch to limit sporulation the following season.
Promote aeration and avoid watering practices that wet the foliage when the fungus is most actively sporulating (late summer to autumn).
For chemical control to be effective, it must take place between July and September; apply three to four treatments at 14–21 day intervals during this time.
Labeled fungicides include: azoxystrobin, thiophanate-methyl, copper hydroxide + mancozeb, mancozeb and triadimefon.

canonical.summary: Symptoms include blighted flower buds, brown and undersized foliage, wilted shoot tips, twig and small branch dieback, and water-soaked fruit lesions that expand to consume the entire fruit; infected blossoms and fruit have a gray-brown powdery coating of spores. Blossom infections can grow into woody tissue forming cankers, and infected fruit dry and shrivel into "mummies" that may persist on the tree.
diagnostic_features: Infected blossoms and fruit have a very conspicuous, gray-brown, powdery coating of spores, which is a sign of the pathogen that can be used to identify the disease in the field. Fruit remains fairly firm and dry relative to a watery (Rhizopus) rot, infected fruit produce tufts of tan conidia and dry into shriveled "mummies," and peaches may show concentric rings of gray sporulation.
look_alikes: watery rot caused by Rhizopus sp.
treatments: Remove infected leaves, shoots and fruit to reduce inoculum within and around the tree, and remove all fruit from the tree and the ground; prune out infected twigs/branches after harvest and in summer
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit in and around the tree, and remove fallen fruit (from thinning or lack of pollination) to reduce rot at harvest
Burn, bury, or otherwise remove infections from the orchard to reduce spores the following season
Destroy wild Prunus spp. in the vicinity of the orchard because they may harbor the fungus
Prune branches to maintain an open canopy for better air circulation and sunlight penetration to promote rapid drying
Control insects that could wound fruit, avoid wounding fruit during harvest, and cool fruit rapidly after harvest
Use moderate amounts of nitrogen fertilizer
A short (2.5 min) soak in hot water (122°F) has reduced postharvest decay in nectarines and peaches

Apply fungicides to control the blossom blight phase (most important): begin just before buds open (pink/white), at early popcorn, full bloom, and/or petal fall, and protect fruit during the ~3 weeks before harvest
Alternate or tank-mix fungicides from different groups with different modes of action to reduce resistance

Labeled fungicides include: calcium polysulfide, copper hydroxide/copper products (Kocide), sulfur, lime sulfur, fenarimol, iprodione (Rovral), mancozeb, propiconazole (Orbit), thiophanate-methyl (Topsin-M), ziram, azoxystrobin (Abound, Heritage), boscalid/pyraclostrobin (Pristine), chlorothalonil (Bravo, Echo, Fung-onil), fenhexamid (Elevate), captan, fenbuconazole (Indar), tebuconazole (Elite), myclobutanil (Nova), and dicloran (Botran)
Biological control: Botector (Aureobasidium pullulans strains DSM 14940 and 14941)

diagnostic_features: White-to-grayish fungal growth (sporulation) on either the lower or upper surfaces of leaves and on newer portions of stem.
treatments: Scout plants carefully for symptoms, especially the undersides of leaves and any stock plants or plants held over from the previous year.
Immediately remove and discard infected plants.
Heat and vent greenhouses late in the day to lower relative humidity at night; maintain adequate fertility.
Ensure good air circulation by staking and/or selective pruning; avoid overcrowding, overwatering, and poorly drained soil; eliminate weeds.
Replace overhead watering with drip or soaker irrigation; sanitation—bag or burn infected material, do not compost, sterilize tools, remove debris in fall.
Choose disease-resistant cultivars; protective applications are important, particularly when the disease has been a problem in previous years.
Once the disease is detected, apply two to three times at the closest intervals allowed, and rotate between chemicals to reduce fungicide resistance.

canonical.summary: Disease begins at the tip of the foliage and progresses toward the leaf base, with foliage turning from green to yellowish to dark brown that can look almost black; lower, older foliage is most affected, smaller twigs may be killed, and tiny black fruiting bodies develop on affected foliage.
diagnostic_features: Tiny black spore-forming fruiting bodies that, examined with a hand lens, resemble short, black strings on the affected foliage.
treatments: Prune out killed foliage and, if necessary, the twigs as soon as possible in the spring (prune when conditions and foliage are dry).
Reduce winter injury by minimizing dehydration.
Do not allow snow to accumulate or remain up and around the base of the plant for any length of time, especially during melting.
Avoid crowding/overcrowding conifers when planting; provide enough space for sufficient sunlight and increased air circulation.
Protect plants from mechanical injury.
Provide good growing conditions and appropriate cultural care to keep plants vigorous.
After cuts, wipe cutting blades clean and spray them with bleach, or dip them in diluted bleach, after cutting through infected shoots.

Fungicide application is generally not recommended in landscapes; in plant nurseries where the disease has been a problem, Bordeaux mixture or another copper fungicide is sometimes applied to help prevent this disease.

canonical.summary: The first symptom is die-back of new shoot growth (tip blight); new growth at the tip of the branches turns from light yellow-green to red-brown and finally ash-gray as it dies, with small lesions appearing around the twig and minute black fruiting bodies embedded in the dry, ashen-gray lesions.
diagnostic_features: Small, black pycnidia (the reproductive structures of the causal fungus) can easily be seen on dead branches with the unaided eye or with a hand lens; the fungus only kills the new growth, with infection starting on immature scale leaves or needles while mature needles are resistant.
treatments: Plant only resistant juniper species, varieties, and cultivars.
Prune out and destroy (burn or bury) diseased branches as they appear; always prune in dry weather and cut four to six inches below obviously diseased areas on each branch.
Restrict pruning and shearing to the dry conditions of mid-June to mid-July; do not use infected branches or needles as mulch.
Decontaminate/sterilize pruning tools between cuts and between plants by treating for at least 30 seconds with a 10% bleach solution or (preferably) 70% rubbing alcohol.
Do not plant conifers in poorly drained sites or heavily shaded areas, and avoid wounding or injuring when planting or cultivating.
Do not overcrowd plantings; provide adequate spacing for good air circulation and rapid drying of foliage.
Do not prune or shear conifers excessively, as this stimulates excessive new, susceptible growth.
Avoid overhead sprinklers; use a soaker or drip hose, or if overhead water must be used, water early in the day to allow fast drying of plant tissue.

For particularly susceptible junipers, combine pruning with copper- or mancozeb-containing fungicides, applied at seven to 21 day intervals during rapid growth in spring; repeat applications are necessary as long as succulent new growth is present with wet weather.
In natural, established plantings the disease generally does not require chemical control, and fungicide applications may be avoided by following good Integrated Pest Management practices.

Reapplications can be made at labeled intervals until needles are fully developed

canonical.summary: Browning of needles on new shoots as they grow from the fascicle sheath, with the shoots curling and dying; small drops of resin ooze from shoot buds in early spring. Dead needles often fade to gray and remain attached, and repeated infections over several years can make the majority of the tree look brown with entire branches dying and the tree becoming deformed.
diagnostic_features: Tiny black fungal fruiting bodies (pycnidia) form on the surface of infected needles (often found under the needle sheaths, especially below the sheath at the base of the needles) and on infected cone scales; these signs are a telltale way to confirm the disease. Lower branches tend to be more severely infected because spores are washed down through the tree by rain.
treatments: Apply a fungicide to the entire crown (especially the lower branches) as the buds begin to swell at bud break, with additional applications about 2 weeks later (or two more applications at 10-day intervals); sprays at other times are not effective.
Use fungicides such as thiophanate-methyl (e.g. Cleary's 3336, OHP 6672), propiconazole (e.g. Banner MAXX), azoxystrobin (Heritage), or Bordeaux mix.
Do not plant healthy 2- or 3-needled pines near older infected pines; ensure no nearby sources of inoculum for nursery seedlings or Christmas tree plantations.
Promote tree vigor by protecting from environmental stresses, insect attack, and injuries, including deep watering during droughts.
Do not use high-nitrogen fertilizers on pines.
Avoid planting too close to other plants in a way that limits airflow.

Prune infected branches (making the cut at least two feet below visible symptoms); avoid pruning/shearing in spring or during wet weather, and disinfest pruning tools between cuts with bleach or 70% alcohol.
Follow pruning with sanitation: remove and destroy infected needles and cones, and collect and dispose of fallen cones.

Salvage heavily infected and dead trees quickly before they lose quality.

Remove and destroy diseased plant parts both during the season (especially spent flowers) and at the end of the season.

canonical.summary: Darkened, water-soaked lesions with defined margins near the stem-end of the tuber; cut tubers show a characteristic pink/salmon color and ammonia-like odor on exposure to air. diagnostic_features: When an infected tuber is cut, the rotted portion is delineated by a dark line at its margin; with exposure to air the surface of the decay turns a salmon pink color, which later turns to brown and then finally black. treatments: Avoid prolonged saturation of soils during irrigation, provide good drainage, and avoid excessive soil moisture especially late in the season

Rotate away from susceptible crops (4 years)
Do not bring infected tubers into storage if possible; remove wet tubers from storage
Use high air flow initially in storage to allow for healing and remove excess moisture from the pile
Maintain good airflow, appropriate humidity, and low temperatures during storage (fungus is inactive below 40°F)
In areas where pink rot is a problem, apply fungicide 2 and 4 weeks before harvest; one application at flowering with a second two weeks later has shown benefit
New in-furrow application at planting reduces cost over two aerial applications

summary.value: Darkened, water-soaked lesions with defined margins near the stem-end of the tuber; cut tubers show a characteristic pink/salmon color and ammonia-like odor on exposure to air. Internal rotted tissue is a dirty, creamy white at first, appearing water soaked yet leathery, turning pink and later darker brown. Vines may appear stunted or wilted with leaf yellowing and drying.
summary.quote: The soilborne pathogen causes darkened, water-soaked lesions with defined margins near the stem-end of the tuber, and is often identified by the characteristic pink/salmon color and ammonia-like odor of a potato cut and exposed to air after 20-30 minutes. Potato vines can also appear stunted or wilted later in the season, with noticeable leaf yellowing and drying as the wilt moves up the stem.

diagnostic_features.value: When an infected tuber is cut, the rotted portion is delineated by a dark line at its margin; with exposure to air the surface of the decay turns a salmon pink color, which later turns to brown and then finally black. There is a definite margin between rotted and healthy tissue, and the organism infects the whole tuber out to the surface rather than causing a cavity.
diagnostic_features.quote: When an infected tuber is cut, the rotted portion is delineated by a dark line at its margin. With exposure to air, the surface of the decay turns a salmon pink color, which later turns to brown and then finally black.

treatments.value: Avoid prolonged saturation of soils during irrigation, provide good drainage, and avoid excessive soil moisture especially late in the season; Minimize wounding and avoid bruising during harvest; Avoid harvesting wet tubers, tubers with pulp temperatures above 65°F, or harvesting in hot conditions; Scout regularly, especially in waterlogged parts of a field; Destroy infested plant debris and rogue volunteer plants; Rotate away from susceptible crops (4 years); Do not bring infected tubers into storage if possible; remove wet tubers from storage; Use high air flow initially in storage to allow for healing and remove excess moisture from the pile; Maintain good airflow, appropriate humidity, and low temperatures during storage (fungus is inactive below 40°F); In areas where pink rot is a problem, apply fungicide 2 and 4 weeks before harvest; one application at flowering with a second two weeks later has shown benefit; New in-furrow application at planting reduces cost over two aerial applications; MEFENOXAM/MANCOZEB (Ridomil Gold MZ, Group 4 + M3) — first application at flowering/nickel-size tubers and another 14 days later; MEFENOXAM/CHLOROTHALONIL (Ridomil Gold Bravo SC, Group 4 + M5) — first application at flowering and another 14 days later; Ridomil Gold SL (Group 4) as a broadcast or band treatment incorporated preplant or at planting; Ridomil Gold Copper (Group 4 + M1) when tubers are nickel-size with a second application two weeks later under high pressure; Quadris Ridomil Gold (Group 11 + 4) applied in-furrow; Orondis Gold (Group 49 + 4) as an in-furrow application at planting; Elumin (Group 22) in-furrow then side-dressed after at least a 25-day interval; Ranman (Group 21) in-furrow at planting or at hilling (Idaho only, SLN ID-060011); Amplitude ST as in-furrow, seed-piece, or chemigation treatment; canonical.summary: Early infections cause pale green leaves that cluster and cup upwards, followed by wilting of the whole plant; affected plants show decaying outer tissue at the crown and a white mat of mycelium at the base of the stem at the soil line, with small white-to-tan sclerotia maturing to dark brown. Fruit in contact with the soil becomes soft, water-soaked, and covered with dense white fan-like fungal growth.
diagnostic_features: A white mat of mycelium at the base of the stem at the soil line, with small spherical white-to-tan sclerotia (0.5 to 2 mm) that turn yellow then dark brown; later symptoms are distinguished from other soilborne diseases by the presence of white mycelium and brown sclerotia at the base of the stem.
treatments: Space plants for air circulation and rapid drying.
Promptly remove and destroy diseased plant material during the growing season.
Manage weeds and potential alternative hosts.
Avoid movement of infested soil to clean fields.
Promptly destroy crop residues after harvest.
Deep plow / deep turn (>4 inches) to bury residual inoculum.
Rotate with nonhost crops for at least 3 years; rotation with certain graminaceous crops can reduce inoculum.
Avoid fields with a history of crops that host S. rolfsii.
Avoid damaging fruit and depositing soil over runners.
Soil solarization (reduces sclerotia viability at 50-55C / 122-131F for up to 6 hours).
Anaerobic soil disinfestation.
Use certified, pathogen-free seed.
Scout to detect infections, followed by plant removal.
Biological control agents such as Trichoderma harzianum, Trichoderma viride, and certain mycorrhizal fungi.
Soil fumigants including chloropicrin, metam-sodium, and allyl isothiocyanate.
Pre-plant fungicides: pentachloronitrobenzene (PCNB) and flutolanil.
Strobilurins: pyraclostrobin, azoxystrobin, and fluoxastrobin.
SDHI-containing: fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin and penthiopyrad.
Triazoles: tebuconazole and prothioconazole.
Fungicidal/chemical control is often limited, variable, and rarely practical or effective.

canonical.summary: On potato, TSWV causes leaf spots with a target appearance similar to early blight but smaller and clustered, with clustering producing large dark brown to black areas (often at the leaf base); leaves may show yellow, brown or black ringspots, sometimes target-like, and distorted growth. Stems and petioles develop dark brown areas / black streaks, growing points can be killed, and branch tip dieback occurs. Tubers can show surface rings or dark patches and internal discolored patches, rings, spots or flecks.
diagnostic_features: Leaf spots are smaller than early blight and tend to be clustered, with affected leaves showing large dark brown to black areas more often at the leaf base; ringspots can form a concentric, target-like pattern with stem streaking; tubers can show surface rings or dark patches and internal discoloration. A distinguishing field clue from fungal diseases is that symptomless plants typically occur next to affected plants.
treatments: There is no known cure; remove and destroy infected plants (burn where allowed, deep bury, or hot compost) to eliminate the virus reservoir
Control thrips vectors using chemical and/or biological products, and monitor with blue and yellow sticky cards placed above plants and near doors and vents
Exclude thrips with 400-mesh screens on vents and limit thrips movement on clothing by avoiding attractive colors (pink, blue, yellow, white, green)
Keep weeds under control in and outside greenhouses to eliminate TSWV and thrips reservoirs
Prevent introduction by carefully inspecting new plants for thrips and TSWV
Test suspect plants for TSWV using dipstick tests (Agdia, Inc.) or by submitting samples to a plant disease diagnostic clinic
Routinely decontaminate items contacting plants (pruners, knives, pots, work surfaces) for at least one minute with Alconox plus sodium dodecyl sulfate, or trisodium phosphate, solutions
Use resistant or tolerant potato varieties to reduce yield losses

Growing points can be killed.

canonical.summary: Fruit lesions are the most common symptom — initially small, depressed, and circular, becoming larger with salmon to pink-colored spore mats that appear wet and gelatinous, eventually rotting the entire fruit.
diagnostic_features: Circular, sunken lesions on fruit producing pink to orange (salmon) spore masses in the center under humid conditions, surrounded by concentric circles, with spiked black spore masses (acervuli) visible in the center of lesions.
treatments: Use pathogen-free / certified clean seed and clean transplants
Inspect pepper transplants before planting and discard any showing water-soaked lesions or soft stem decay
Rotate crops to non-solanaceous plants for 2-3 years (at least two years); avoid strawberry as it is an alternative host
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or systems that limit water splash, and avoid field operations when plants are wet
Scout fields regularly and remove infected fruit/plants immediately
Destroy crop residue: mow fields immediately after harvest and incorporate debris into the soil to speed breakdown
Use black plastic or mulch as a barrier between soil-borne pathogen and plants
Maintain adequate field drainage to reduce moisture and water-logging
Clean and disinfect equipment (irrigation hoses, baskets, tractors, trucks, wagons), trays and greenhouse tools between uses/before storage
Apply fungicides preventatively starting at first fruit set / flowering, continuing on a 7-to-10-day interval as fruit ripens, rotating modes of action to avoid resistance

Effective fungicides include FRAC group 11 products (Quadris, Quadris Top, Aprovia Top) and contact fungicides with chlorothalonil (Bravo, Echo, Equus, Initiate) or mancozeb (Dithane, Manzate, Penncozeb)
OMRI-approved / copper fungicide applications (main option for home gardeners)
Use host resistance where available
